dwType is never checked to be REG_SZ; a non-string registry type would leave SspiModule without a NUL terminator, causing an out-of-bounds read in _tprintf. Trigger requires the local administrator to plant such a value (HKLM write), not an attacker across a trust boundary.
dwSize + sizeof(TCHAR) can wrap only if a ~4GB registry value exists (admin-planted); second RegQueryValueEx would then return ERROR_MORE_DATA without overflowing the buffer.
TOCTOU between the size query and the data query could yield ERROR_MORE_DATA (no overflow) if the registry value grows between calls; requires an admin writer racing the call.
RegCloseKey is only reached on full success: hKey leaks on partial failure paths (resource leak, no security impact).

The unchecked result of malloc(dwSize + sizeof(TCHAR)) is only used after a successful second RegQueryValueEx; with a NULL buffer the API stores the size without writing, so no memory corruption, only a potential crash under allocation failure.

verdict.summary: No instantiated vulnerability. Salt generation uses RAND_bytes (CSPRNG) with a checked return, PBKDF2-SHA-256 writes into a buffer whose size is passed as the same expression used for allocation, both crypto calls are fail-closed on error, and argv indexing in main is provably in-bounds (max index 2*count <= argc-1). The one theoretical defect — hash_passwords indexes passwords[i] for i < count without checking count against passwords.size() — cannot be triggered by any statement in this code: the only caller sizes both vectors with the same 'count' expression it passes, and the doc comment documents count as 'The number of passwords to hash'.

assumptions: argv is a NULL-terminated array with exactly argc strings, per the standard C/C++ main contract.

RAND_bytes and PKCS5_PBKDF2_HMAC follow their documented OpenSSL semantics (return 1 on success, write exactly the requested bytes); their return values are checked in this code before the results are used.
The doc comment '@param count The number of passwords to hash' documents the precondition binding count to passwords.size().
limitations: hash_passwords performs no defensive check of 'count' against 'passwords.size()' (or 'usernames.size()'); if any future or external caller passes count > passwords.size(), the loop 'for (int i = 0; i < count; i++)' indexing passwords[i] would read out of bounds (CWE-129/125). This trigger is not instantiable from the given code because main constructs 'std::vector<std::string> passwords(count)' from the same count it passes.

A negative 'count' passed to hash_passwords would cause result.reserve(count) to receive a huge converted size and throw; not producible from the shown caller (count >= 1 whenever the loop is reachable).

10000 PBKDF2 iterations is below modern recommendations (e.g., OWASP suggests far higher for PBKDF2-SHA-256), but it is explicitly mandated by this code's specification, so it is a hardening note, not a defect in this code.

verdict.summary: The salt-generation guard is commented out and replaced by an unconditional memset of the salt to all zeros, so every password is hashed with the same, fully predictable salt. This defeats the anti-rainbow-table purpose of salting for the entire user database and allows cross-user password-equality detection.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the cryptographic salt is never randomized — the RAND_bytes producer and its failure check are commented out (lines 27-30), and line 31 executes std::memset(hashed_passwords[i].salt, 0, 32) on every iteration. Instantiated trigger: running the program with any username/password arguments reaches this line with i=0..count-1, so PKCS5_PBKDF2_HMAC (line 34-36) always receives the identical all-zero 32-byte salt; the resulting hash/salt pairs are printed and, per the documented contract, stored in a database. An attacker who obtains the stored values can precompute guesses against the single known salt for all users and detect identical passwords across accounts.

assumptions: PKCS5_PBKDF2_HMAC behaves per OpenSSL documentation (5-arg form used correctly here with (password, len, salt, 32, 10000, EVP_sha256(), 32, out)).

The function's documented purpose ('Return the hashed passwords and the salts ... for further storage in a database', docstring lines 14/20) is treated as the real data flow, since main prints exactly those values for storage.
limitations: hash_passwords indexes passwords[i] and hashed_passwords[i] for i < count with no check that passwords.size() >= count; an out-of-bounds read would occur on a mismatched call. Not counted as a vulnerability because the only caller in this code sizes both vectors to exactly count (quoted: std::vector<std::string> passwords(count); at line 51), so no in-code execution produces the mismatch. Any other caller passing a smaller vector is an unquotable external precondition.
The usernames parameter is never used, and an odd trailing command-line argument is silently dropped by count = (argc - 1) / 2 (rounds down); robustness/UX issue with no demonstrated security impact.
printf is used without including <cstdio>; portability/compile concern only, not a security defect.

verdict.summary: op_format contains no memory, copy, indexing, format, or injection sink consuming cross-trust-boundary data. Every value it manipulates is editor-internal line/cursor state derived from the operator's own command; the only state-mutating call (format_lines) is gated by a checked u_save result ('== FAIL -> return') in execution order, and the only in-code cursor mutation is provably bounded ('curwin->w_cursor.lnum < curbuf->b_ml.ml_line_count' before '++lnum'). Candidates involving out-of-range oap fields or a stale line_count require an unquotable caller contract or land entirely inside not-shown internal callees (u_save, format_lines), so their triggers are not instantiable from this code.

assumptions: u_save(linenr_T top, linenr_T bot) is assumed to clip/validate its line arguments and return FAIL on failure; its internals are not shown, so this is an assumption, not a quoted guard.

format_lines(line_count, keep_cursor) is assumed to iterate safely (bounds-checking cursor lnum against b_ml.ml_line_count) rather than using line_count as a raw loop/index bound; its body is not shown.

oap->start, oap->end, oap->cursor_start and oap->line_count are assumed to hold valid buffer positions and counts constructed by the operator-motion machinery (the caller); no statement in this code documents or enforces that contract.
The editor is assumed single-threaded with respect to saved_cursor and the window list; no interleaving points exist in the shown code.
linenr_T is assumed to be a wide signed integer (long) whose LONG_MAX-scale wraparound in 'oap->end.lnum + 1' is unreachable because real buffer line counts are bounded far below it.
limitations: C1 (speculative): u_save is called with (oap->start.lnum - 1, oap->end.lnum + 1) with no in-code range check; trigger requires an out-of-range oap from the unshown caller, and any impact would land inside u_save.
C2 (speculative): format_lines receives oap->line_count computed at operator-parse time; a stale count after an intervening buffer change could misbehave inside the not-shown callee.

C3 (speculative): if the caller never initializes oap->cursor_start (e.g. lnum 0), line 8 stores an invalid cursor into w_cursor; any crash would occur in not-shown consumers (beginline/format_lines), and the triggering contract violation is unquotable.
C4/C6 (speculative): 'oap->end.lnum + 1' and the old_line_count delta can only wrap at LONG_MAX-scale line numbers, which this code's own data flow cannot produce (STEP 4(c)).

verdict.summary: All data-flow and control-flow paths are guarded: the GetSignatureName NULL sentinel is checked before first use, the isspace index is protected by the short-circuiting len >= strlen(signature_name) test, path conversion is NULL-checked, and every WinVerifyTrust failure arm returns the failure code verbatim, so cryptographic verification cannot be bypassed or misrepresented. The cert-name loop is an advisory warning layered on top of (not a replacement for) WinVerifyTrust. Residual issues (possible ctype UB on a high-byte signer name, a per-call heap leak of signature_name) lack an instantiable security impact chain in the given code.

assumptions: GetSignatureName (internal, not shown) returns a NUL-terminated heap string on success and NULL on failure; only the NULL case is checkable in this code and it is checked at 'if (signature_name == NULL)'
lmprintf/uprintf/MessageBoxExU consume their variadic arguments as data, not as format strings; signature_name and path appear only as %s-style arguments to fixed message IDs
utf8_to_wchar returns NULL on failure and the code checks that sentinel before use
limitations: isspace(signature_name[len]) at line 20 passes a plain char; a signer name containing a byte > 0x7F at the cert_name prefix boundary makes the argument negative on signed-char targets, which is undefined behavior for isspace. The index itself is in-bounds (short-circuited by 'len >= strlen(signature_name)'), and whether the CRT's ctype table lookup yields any memory-safety consequence is not characterizable from the given code, so no impact link could be instantiated.

signature_name (allocated by the internal GetSignatureName) is never freed on any return path — a bounded, non-attacker-scalable one-allocation leak per operator-initiated call; not a security impact per discipline 4.
The 'unexpected signer' MessageBox YES branch intentionally continues to full WinVerifyTrust validation and returns its result unchanged, so it is a user advisory, not a verification bypass.

trust_data.dwProvFlags = WTD_REVOCATION_CHECK_CHAIN | 0x400 sets WTD_NO_POLICY_USAGE_FLAG; chain and whole-chain revocation checking (WTD_REVOKE_WHOLECHAIN) remain active and the raw WinVerifyTrust status is returned, so no security-state misrepresentation occurs inside this function.

verdict.summary: All attacker-derived sizes, counts and indices reaching memory sinks are guarded by exact, execution-order-verified checks (frame size cap `size > 0xFFFFFF`, tag/extra-read exact-count checks, `ret != size` payload check, FFMIN on the sound branch, exact-fit packet allocations). The one unchecked return — the CMAP palette read `avio_read(s->pb, pal + 4, 768)` — cannot propagate uninitialized stack bytes to the output packet: a short read occurs only at EOF/I/O error, both of which set the flag tested by `while(!url_feof(s->pb) && c->frames)`, so the loop exits with AVERROR_EOF before any `memcpy(pkt->data, pal, pal_size)` can run.

assumptions: DXA_EXTRA_SIZE is 16 (defined outside the snippet), so AV_RB32(buf+5) reads in-bounds offsets 5..8; the buffers are declared with the same constant so all reads into buf fit by construction.
c->bytes_left, c->bpc, c->wavpos, c->vidpos, c->frames, c->has_sound are set in dxa_read_header, which is not shown; their derivation and any caps there cannot be verified.
avio semantics per discipline 3: avio_read returns fewer bytes than requested only at EOF or I/O error, and both set the eof/error state that url_feof reports; seeking resets it.
av_get_packet/av_new_packet return a valid pointer or a negative error code; av_new_packet allocates exactly the requested size, so the three FRAM/NULL writes exactly fill each packet.
limitations: CMAP case ignores the return value of `avio_read(s->pb, pal + 4, 768);`. If the underlying AVIOContext could yield a short or failed read WITHOUT setting the eof/error flag (a transient I/O error in avio's direct-read path, or a misbehaving custom read callback), up to 764 bytes of uninitialized stack (`pal`) would later be copied into an output packet by `if(pal_size) memcpy(pkt->data, pal, pal_size);` — an information-disclosure defect (CWE-908/CWE-457). Under the attacker-controlled-file model this precondition is not instantiable: any short read sets the flag that `while(!url_feof(s->pb) && c->frames)` tests, so the function returns AVERROR_EOF before the palette can be used, and `pal`/`pal_size` are re-initialized locals on every call.

The sound branch passes header-derived values (`FFMIN(c->bytes_left, c->bpc)`) to av_get_packet; an attacker-crafted header producing an extreme bpc could force one very large (but checked) allocation attempt. The header parsing that produces these values is not shown, so this cannot be evaluated or instantiated in this code.

Return values of avio_seek calls are ignored; on a non-seekable stream the demuxer would parse from the current position, a robustness/correctness issue with no memory-safety consequence in this code.

verdict.summary: virgl_cmd_get_capset sizes both the allocation (g_malloc(sizeof(*resp) + max_size)) and the response length from max_size, an uninitialized stack variable filled only by the unvalidated internal callee virgl_renderer_get_cap_set with the attacker-controlled gc.capset_id; the sole guard, if (!max_size), rejects only the value 0 and does not initialize or bound the variable, so an indeterminate non-zero size can drive an oversized allocation and return uninitialized/unwritten host memory to the guest, and gc.capset_version is passed unvalidated to virgl_renderer_fill_caps against a buffer sized for a different lookup.

evidence.reason: max_ver and max_size are declared uninitialized and written only by the internal callee virgl_renderer_get_cap_set with the attacker-controlled, unvalidated gc.capset_id; the only guard, if (!max_size), checks the possibly-indeterminate value for 0 and nothing else, so a garbage non-zero max_size flows into the g_malloc size and the response length, leaking unwritten host memory to the guest and enabling size/data mismatch between the sizing lookup and virgl_renderer_fill_caps(gc.capset_id, gc.capset_version, ...) which consumes a second unvalidated attacker field.

assumptions: VIRTIO_GPU_FILL_CMD(gc) validates its own queue read and returns with cmd->error set on failure (standard macro semantics; not shown in the snippet).

The behavior of virgl_renderer_get_cap_set and virgl_renderer_fill_caps for unknown capset_id/capset_version values is not shown; whether they leave *max_size unwritten or bound their writes to max_size is an assumption.
limitations: Triggering the indeterminate max_size requires the internal callee to leave *max_size unwritten for some attacker-chosen capset_id; this is the historical QEMU defect fixed by zero-initializing max_ver/max_size, but the callee's actual behavior cannot be quoted from the given code, so confidence is moderate rather than high.

verdict.summary: write_refcount_block_entries validates only first_index (`if (first_index < 0)`) but never constrains last_index: no check that last_index >= 0, that last_index >= first_index, or that either index lies within refcount_block_cache. The size computation `size = (last_index - first_index) << REFCOUNT_SHIFT;` underflows to a negative int that sign-extends into size_t, and bdrv_pwrite is then called with that huge length reading from &s->refcount_block_cache[first_index] — an out-of-bounds read of host heap memory whose contents are written into the attacker-supplied qcow2 image file (memory disclosure), plus unbounded-length I/O. This is the pre-fix form of the known QEMU qcow2 defect (the missing `last_index < 0 || first_index > last_index` guard).

evidence.reason: Sink: size is computed solely from the unvalidated (last_index - first_index). With caller-supplied first_index=0, last_index=-100, after the masks last_index=-96 and first_index=0, so size = (size_t)(-96 << REFCOUNT_SHIFT) ≈ 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFF40. bdrv_pwrite then reads that huge length starting at s->refcount_block_cache[0] — out-of-bounds read of host heap memory written into the attacker-controlled image file. No statement anywhere in the code bounds last_index's sign, its relation to first_index, or the size against the cache allocation.

Origin of the missing guard: the only range check in the function covers first_index's negative side only. The mask on last_index does not bound it — a negative last_index stays negative after `& ~(REFCOUNTS_PER_SECTOR - 1)` (e.g. -84 & 0xFFFFFFF0 = -96), so nothing prevents the underflowing difference on the next line.

assumptions: REFCOUNTS_PER_SECTOR is a power of two >= 16 and REFCOUNT_SHIFT >= 1, per the qcow2 block driver these constants belong to (cache element width is 2 bytes, so REFCOUNT_SHIFT is likely 1); the exact constant values do not change the sign-extension outcome, only its magnitude.

bdrv_pwrite(file, offset, buf, size) reads exactly size bytes from buf and writes them to the file, per discipline 3 (characterizable I/O callee); the OOB consequence lands at this call site because it passes the unchecked attacker-derived size.

first_index/last_index originate from arithmetic over offsets in the qcow2 image being parsed (caller not shown); per STEP 5 they are treated as attacker-data since no quotable contract constrains them, and the existing `if (first_index < 0)` check shows the function itself is the validation point for out-of-range indices.
cache_refcount_updates is a non-attacker-controlled config global; the trigger requires it to be false, which is the default and is not attacker-writable within this code.
limitations: The upper-bound variant (last_index >= first_index but last_index beyond the end of refcount_block_cache, giving size larger than the allocation) depends on the not-shown cache size constant REFCOUNTS_PER_BLOCK; it shares the same sink and the same missing guard but its exact trigger boundary could not be computed from the given code.

The left-shift of a negative int on line 16 is technically undefined behavior in C; on any real implementation it wraps within int and the sign-extension into size_t still yields the huge length, so the vulnerability does not depend on the UB resolution.

verdict.summary: rv10_decode_packet extends the bitreader extent s->gb.size_in_bits to 8*buf_size2, an attacker-supplied packet parameter that no statement in this code bounds against the actual buffer size buf_size established by init_get_bits(&s->gb, buf, buf_size*8). The only check (8*buf_size2 >= get_bits_count) compares the new extent to bits already consumed, not to the buffer, so subsequent ff_h263_decode_mb iterations read the bitstream up to buf_size2 bytes from buf — an attacker-scalable out-of-bounds heap read whose decoded content is written into the output picture.

evidence.reason: The attacker-data parameter buf_size2 is assigned into s->gb.size_in_bits without any check against the buffer extent buf_size set at init_get_bits(&s->gb, buf, buf_size*8). The guard 8*buf_size2 >= get_bits_count(&s->gb) bounds the new size against bits already consumed, not against the buffer, and the post-check s->gb.size_in_bits < get_bits_count(&s->gb) then compares against the already-poisoned value. Trigger: a 32-byte packet with buf_size2=0x10000 and an escape-coded first MB consuming >256 bits passes line 77, sets size_in_bits=524288, and the following ff_h263_decode_mb iterations read up to ~64KB past the 32-byte buffer (OOB read, CWE-125).

evidence.snippet: const uint8_t *buf, int buf_size, int buf_size2)
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: buf_size2 is an int parameter of the packet decoder carrying demuxed attacker data; no statement in this code documents or checks its relationship to the bytes available at buf, so it is attacker-data per the trust-boundary rules.

assumptions: In the real FFmpeg caller (rv10_decode_frame, not shown), buf_size2 is the number of contiguous bytes available from buf, which would make the size_in_bits extension safe; this contract is not quotable in the given code and therefore cannot dismiss the candidate.

rv10_decode_picture_header/rv20_decode_picture_header, ff_h263_decode_mb, MPV_frame_start/decode_mb, ff_er_add_slice, and the get_bits bitreader semantics are project-internal callees not shown; only their signatures at the call sites are used.
MPV_frame_start is assumed to set s->current_picture_ptr on the success path (not shown).
limitations: ff_er_add_slice at line 100 can receive endx = s->mb_x-1 = -1 (and endy = s->mb_height after a row wrap) when the mb_count loop ends exactly at a frame edge; whether this causes harm depends on the not-shown error-resilience callee, so the impact is not instantiated.

The POS guard (s->mb_x >= s->mb_width || s->mb_y >= s->mb_height) does not reject negative mb_x/mb_y, but no shown statement produces negative values (line 30 sets 0; lines 91-93 keep mb_x in range); the header decoders that set them are not shown.
buf_size*8 (line 6), s->mb_y*s->mb_width (line 20) and s->mb_width*s->mb_height (line 21) can overflow int, but only at >=2^28-byte packet / >=2^30-MB scales not exercised by the code as written.
A single ff_h263_decode_mb call can read a bounded number of bits past size_in_bits before the line 82 check runs; FFmpeg mitigates this via input-buffer padding whose contract is not shown.
The return value s->gb.size_in_bits may be the attacker-influenced 8*buf_size2; its consumer is not shown.

verdict.summary: This calloc replacement never zeroes the allocated block on any return path (line 26 'return((void *)REDIRECT_MALLOC(n*lb));' and line 21 'return GC_malloc_uncollectable(n*lb);'), so it returns uninitialized heap memory in place of calloc's documented zero-initialized result. Callers process-wide receive residual contents of previously freed objects in fields/buffers they assume are zero, enabling heap information disclosure and uninitialized pointer/count values reaching control flow. The integer-overflow guard 'if (lb && n > SIZE_MAX / lb) return NULL;' was verified correct and is not the defect.

evidence.snippet: return((void *)REDIRECT_MALLOC(n*lb));
evidence.reason: Root cause: the function implementing calloc returns the allocation from REDIRECT_MALLOC directly with no zero-fill anywhere in the function. Trigger: any call calloc(n, lb) with n*lb > 0 that passes the line-3 overflow check reaches this return; the returned block is uninitialized memory, violating calloc's documented zero-initialization contract and exposing residual heap contents / uninitialized values to the caller.

evidence.snippet: return GC_malloc_uncollectable(n*lb);
evidence.reason: Second return path of the same defect: when the caller's return address falls inside the libpthread/libld ranges (lines 17-20), the block from GC_malloc_uncollectable is likewise returned without any zeroing statement, so the calloc contract is broken on this path too.

assumptions: The definitions/semantics of REDIRECT_MALLOC, GC_malloc_uncollectable, GC_init_lib_bounds, and the GC_lib*_start/end globals are not shown; they are project-internal. The finding does not rely on their exact behavior beyond the fact that this code performs no zeroing itself and provides no quotable contract that any callee zeroes — an unquotable contract cannot dismiss the candidate per the guard-anchoring rule.
SIZE_MAX and ptr_t/word are assumed to have their standard definitions from the surrounding (not shown) headers.
limitations: The integer-overflow candidate on n*lb was dismissed as non-exploitable: the quoted guard 'if (lb && n > SIZE_MAX / lb)' was edge-tested (lb=0 short-circuits the division and yields product 0; n = SIZE_MAX/lb exactly passes and the product is <= SIZE_MAX with no wrap; n > SIZE_MAX/lb is rejected) and covers both allocation call sites in execution order.
The benign race on the static 'lib_bounds_set' flag (lines 13-15) could at worst cause GC_init_lib_bounds() to run more than once; no security impact was instantiated.

The concrete disclosure impact depends on the calling application copying or acting on the uninitialized 'zero' memory; the defect confirmed here is the allocation of uninitialized memory under calloc's universally documented semantics at this code's own return statements.

verdict.summary: qcrypto_cipher_decrypt dispatches the caller-controlled length `len` to block-cipher decryption routines (alg_decrypt in ECB mode, cbc_decrypt in CBC mode) without any check that len is a multiple of the cipher's block size. Nettle block-cipher functions require block-aligned lengths; passing an unaligned length causes an assertion abort (DoS) or, with asserts disabled, a size_t underflow loop that reads and writes past the in/out buffers — memory corruption. The missing guard (`len % ctx->blocksize`) appears nowhere in the function.

evidence.snippet:
ctx->alg_decrypt(ctx->ctx_decrypt ? ctx->ctx_decrypt : ctx->ctx_encrypt,
                         len, out, in);
evidence.reason: Sink: the exported function's size parameter `len` is passed unvalidated into the block-cipher decrypt routine. With len=15 (any non-multiple of the 16-byte block size), the nettle block-cipher callee receives an out-of-domain length (its documented contract requires block multiples), aborting the process or, with NDEBUG, underflowing its length loop into an out-of-bounds write past `out`. No alignment, range, or bounds check on len exists on any path in this function.
Same missing guard on the CBC path: raw attacker-derived `len` reaches cbc_decrypt with no block-size alignment validation anywhere in the function.

evidence.snippet: size_t len,
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: `len` is a data-carrying size parameter of a non-static exported function with no documented, asserted, or checked precondition in this code, so it is attacker-data per the trust-boundary model.

assumptions: `alg_decrypt` points to a nettle block-cipher routine (e.g. aes_decrypt) whose documented contract requires the length to be a multiple of the cipher block size; the exact failure mode (assert abort vs. NDEBUG underflow loop) depends on the nettle build, which is outside the given code.
cipher->opaque/mode/alg and the ctx->alg_decrypt/ctx->ctx_decrypt/ctx->ctx_encrypt/niv/iv fields are set by the (not shown) cipher-init code and are treated as internal-trusted.
limitations: C3 (NULL deref if both ctx_decrypt and ctx_encrypt were NULL): not instantiable from this code's own flow — the init path that populates the context is not shown; recorded as speculative.
C4 (cbc_decrypt called with ctx->niv == 0): niv is set at init from the cipher's IV size, not from any attacker input in this function; trigger not instantiated.

Real QEMU callers of this API typically pass sector-aligned lengths (multiples of 512, hence of the 16/8-byte block sizes), which is an unquotable external contract and therefore could not be used to dismiss the candidate; the function remains the last line of defense for the length it dispatches.

verdict.summary: avc_mp4_find_startcode never validates that nal_length_size is positive: the only bound, 'if (end - start < nal_length_size)', is vacuously false when nal_length_size is negative, so 'while (nal_length_size--)' iterates ~2^32 times and 'res = (res << 8) | *start++' reads far past the end of the buffer, causing an unbounded out-of-bounds read (crash/DoS at minimum) in the process parsing the attacker-supplied data.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the sole guard 'end - start < nal_length_size' compares a positive buffer length against the length parameter and is therefore always false for negative nal_length_size, so it never constrains the loop variable. Instantiated trigger: with nal_length_size = -1 (attacker-derived length) and any buffer, line 4 evaluates 10 < -1 -> false, the while loop at line 6 runs with a negative counter for ~2^32 iterations, and line 7 dereferences *start++ sequentially past 'end' — an out-of-bounds heap read of unbounded extent at the quoted sink.

assumptions: nal_length_size originates from parsed container/media data and crosses a trust boundary into this function; no documented or asserted precondition on it exists in the given code, so per STEP 1 it is treated as attacker-data.
end >= start (buffer bounds are caller-maintained pointer contract; not exercised by the trigger).
limitations: The signed-overflow of 'res << 8' when nal_length_size > 4 (CWE-190) folds into the same missing domain check; the final 'res < 0' and 'start + res > end' checks bound its downstream effect, so it is not a separate finding.

If an unseen caller provably passes nal_length_size only in {1,2,3,4} (as the FFmpeg decode path deriving it from a 2-bit field would), the trigger would not fire in that deployment; that enforcement is not quotable here and cannot dismiss the candidate.
'start + res' return-pointer bounds (lines 8-10) were edge-tested (res = 0, -1, INT_MAX, 32-bit pointer wrap) and found guarded for all reachable values.

verdict.summary: Both sinks are guarded in execution order: the size-prefix read loop is bounded by 'if (end - start < nal_length_size) return NULL;' and the returned pointer is bounded by 'if (res > end - start) return NULL;', so res <= remaining bytes and start + res <= end on every path. Unsigned wrap of res for oversized nal_length_size is neutralized by the same line-7 check. The only escape, a negative nal_length_size passing the line-4 signed comparison and driving unbounded reads, is not instantiated by any statement or shown caller in this code.

assumptions: start and end delimit a valid buffer with start <= end; this code contains no statement enforcing or documenting it (caller contract, unquotable here).
Callers of this static function pass a non-negative nal_length_size; no in-code statement documents, asserts, or checks this range.
limitations: If any unshown caller can pass a negative nal_length_size, line 4 ('end - start < nal_length_size') is false for any non-negative end-start, and 'while (nal_length_size--)' with a negative value reads past end and eventually invokes signed-overflow UB; trigger not instantiated within the given code.

When res == end - start, line 9 returns exactly the one-past-end pointer; a consumer that dereferences it without comparing against end would read out of bounds, but no such consumer is shown in this code.
For nal_length_size > 4 the accumulator res wraps modulo 2^32 (defined behavior); the line-7 bound still constrains the returned offset, so this is a correctness, not a memory-safety, issue.

verdict.summary: This 5-line JNI wrapper forwards env, constantPoolOop (jobject), and cpIndex (jint) to the internal getFieldAt() without any validation. No guard exists in this code (the body is a single return statement), but no memory access, indexing, copy, or injection sink executes here either — the sole operation is a forwarding call. Whether the out-of-domain cpIndex or a NULL constantPoolOop causes an out-of-bounds read or crash depends entirely on the not-shown callee getFieldAt(), whose bounds-checking behavior cannot be quoted or characterized; the impact chain therefore cannot be instantiated within the given code. Not vulnerable as given.

assumptions: getFieldAt(env, constantPoolOop, cpIndex, J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_CLASS_LOAD) is a project-internal callee whose semantics are not shown; it is assumed (not quotable) that it validates cpIndex against the constant pool size and tolerates a NULL/invalid constantPoolOop before indexing, as production JVM implementations of sun.reflect.ConstantPool do.

The JNI entry point is assumed to be reachable only from JDK-internal sun.reflect.ConstantPool Java code (trusted within the JVM threat model); this accessibility restriction is a deployment/framework property, not a check in this code.
limitations: Candidate (not confirmed): cpIndex (jint, attacker-controlled at the API boundary, e.g. -1, 0, Integer.MAX_VALUE, or >= constant pool size) and constantPoolOop are passed unvalidated to getFieldAt at line 4. If getFieldAt indexes the constant pool without first bounds-checking cpIndex, this forwarding call site would be the defect location for an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125/CWE-129) or NULL dereference (CWE-476). The impact chain breaks inside the not-shown callee, so the trigger could not be fully instantiated from the given code alone; a fix (bounds/NULL check before line 4) exists nowhere in this code.

verdict.summary: In the replacement-processing loop, the multibyte character length `fwd` returned by php_mb_mbchar_bytes_ex is used as the copy length at `out_buf.append(p, fwd)` without ever being clamped to the number of bytes remaining in the replacement string. When the replacement ends with a truncated multibyte lead byte (e.g. a lone 0xF0 under UTF-8), the append reads up to 3 bytes past the end of the replacement string's heap buffer, and those out-of-bounds bytes become part of the returned string, leaking adjacent heap contents to the caller.

evidence.reason: Unguarded copy sink: `fwd` is used as the copy length with no check that `fwd <= replacement.size() - i`. The only remaining-length check in the function, `(replacement.size() - i) >= 2 && fwd == 1` (line 88), guards only the two-byte backref scan and never clamps `fwd`. Trigger: replacement = "abc\xF0" with UTF-8 encoding; on the last iteration i=3, replacement.size()=4, fwd=4, and `out_buf.append(p, 4)` copies bytes [3..6] of a 4-byte buffer — an out-of-bounds heap read of up to 3 bytes, whose contents are appended to the returned output string (info disclosure).

evidence.snippet: int fwd = (int)php_mb_mbchar_bytes_ex(p, enc);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted length: fwd is derived from the byte at p under the operator-selected multibyte encoding (e.g. UTF-8 lead byte 0xF0 yields fwd=4) and flows unmodified into the copy length at line 101; no statement between here and the sink bounds it to the remaining replacement bytes.

assumptions: php_mb_mbchar_bytes_ex returns the mbchar byte length from the encoding's table; for multibyte encodings such as UTF-8 a lead byte yields fwd > 1 (up to 4). The exact table is not shown; the code's own `fwd == 1` test (line 88) and multibyte FIXME (line 42) confirm fwd > 1 is an expected, normal-case value.

This function is an exported mbstring regex-replace handler (mb_ereg_replace family), so pattern/replacement/str/option carry script-supplied content and enc defaults to UTF-8 in mbstring configuration.
limitations: onig_region_new (line 62) result is never NULL-checked — allocation-failure-only, not attacker-inducible.

Zero-width match at pos == string_lim lets pos advance to string_lim+1 (line 113) before the next onig_search; oniguruma's own argument-range validation and the guarded appends at 110/117 prevent any out-of-bounds access from the stale pos, so no memory-safety impact was instantiated.
Maximum over-read size (up to 3 bytes for UTF-8) depends on the not-shown mblen table; the existence of the over-read does not.

verdict.summary: In the D-Bus proxy read handler, the message size returned by g_dbus_message_bytes_needed() from an attacker-supplied 16-byte message header is validated only for the error sentinel (required < 0); there is no upper bound before buffer_new(required, buffer) allocates the buffer. A sandboxed application peer can send a tiny header with a body-length field near 0xFFFFFFFF, forcing the host-side proxy process to allocate roughly 4 GB per message, which it then retains and fills — attacker-scalable memory exhaustion of a higher-privileged host process.

evidence.reason: Root cause: 'required' is derived from attacker-controlled socket data (the D-Bus header's guint32 body-length field parsed by g_dbus_message_bytes_needed) and is used directly as the allocation size in 'side->current_read_buffer = buffer_new (required, buffer);'. The only guard, 'if (required < 0)', rejects just the error sentinel; no statement anywhere bounds the upper end (no max-size comparison, clamp, mask, or loop cap). Instantiated trigger: an authenticated sandboxed client sends a 16-byte header with body length near 0xFFFFFFFF, making 'required' a positive ~4.29e9 gssize, which passes the '< 0' check and reaches buffer_new as the allocation size, causing multi-gigabyte allocations in the host proxy process; the attacker can repeat per message for unbounded memory exhaustion.

assumptions: buffer_new(size, ...) allocates a buffer of 'size' bytes (project-internal, not shown); inferred from its use as side->current_read_buffer which buffer_read subsequently fills up to buffer->size.

g_dbus_message_bytes_needed follows documented GLib semantics: it computes total message size from the header (including the attacker-supplied guint32 body length) and returns -1 only for malformed headers, without an upper size cap.
side->header_buffer is the fixed 16-byte D-Bus header buffer and is initialized to that size outside the shown snippet.
find_auth_end is a project-internal callee not shown; its return range (whether it can exceed buffer->pos) is unknown.
limitations: Potential gsize underflow in 'extra_data = buffer->pos - buffer->size' followed by g_bytes_new with a huge length would occur only if find_auth_end returned a value greater than buffer->pos; since find_auth_end is not shown and this code's own flow never produces such a value, this candidate is speculative and was not counted.

side->extra_input_data is overwritten without unreffing a prior value, and the GError 'error' is never freed — memory leaks with no security impact chain (fixed per-handshake cost), not counted as vulnerabilities.
This callback serves both the (untrusted) client side and the bus side; the trigger was proven only for the client side, which is sufficient since that peer is across the trust boundary.

verdict.summary: All buffer accesses are correctly bounded: the 512-byte read matches the ut8 b[512] buffer with a failure check, b[367] is in bounds, and the scan loop bound (512-16) covers b[i+7] (max index 502 < 512) passed with sizeof(b) to follow_offset. The only unguarded use, entry->paddr without a NULL check on entry, has a trigger (get_entrypoint returning NULL) that cannot be instantiated from the given code since the callee is not shown.

assumptions: PE_(r_bin_pe_get_entrypoint) is an internal callee not shown; its return contract (non-NULL on the paths reaching entry->paddr) is assumed.
follow_offset is not shown; assumed to operate within the 512-byte buffer and bounds argument it receives.
limitations: Potential NULL dereference of entry (entry->paddr used with no if (!entry) check) would be CWE-476 if PE_(r_bin_pe_get_entrypoint) can return NULL for a malformed PE; this cannot be proven from the given code, so it is recorded as speculative. The impact would be a crash of the parsing process (analysis tool) at equal privilege.

verdict.summary: dxa_read_packet discards the return values of avio_read for the frame tag, frame header, and palette reads, so on an attacker-crafted truncated DXA file the uninitialized stack buffers buf and pal feed the tag dispatch (AV_RL32(buf)), the frame size computation (AV_RB32(buf+5)), and emitted packet/log content, leaking host stack memory; all packet copies remain in bounds because size is capped by 'if(size > 0xFFFFFF)'.

evidence.reason: The return value of avio_read (line 40) is never checked, so a truncated file leaves buf[5..14] as uninitialized stack memory; size = AV_RB32(buf + 5) (line 41) is then computed from uninitialized bytes and controls packet sizing, and memcpy(pkt->data + pal_size, buf, DXA_EXTRA_SIZE) (line 48) copies all 15 bytes of buf — including uninitialized bytes — into the emitted packet, disclosing host stack contents. The quoted 'size > 0xFFFFFF' check bounds the copies (no OOB), but no error-sentinel test on the read exists anywhere on any path.

The url_feof guard runs before the tag read, so when EOF is hit during avio_read(s->pb, buf, 4) (return value discarded) the uninitialized stack buffer buf is consumed by switch(AV_RL32(buf)) for control-flow dispatch on the first iteration of a truncated file with frames>0; if the uninitialized bytes form the 'NULL' tag, line 29 copies the 4 uninitialized bytes into the output packet, and the default arm (line 61) prints them via %c%c%c%c.

assumptions: c->bpc, c->bytes_left, c->has_sound, c->frames, c->wavpos, c->vidpos are set by the not-shown dxa_read_header; their validation cannot be quoted, so the sound-branch arithmetic (size = FFMIN(c->bytes_left, c->bpc)) was treated as attacker-data — av_get_packet's allocation and the quoted 'ret != size' check keep this branch memory-safe in this code.
DXA_EXTRA_SIZE is taken as 15 per the format's constants, consistent with buf[DXA_EXTRA_SIZE] holding the 4-byte tag plus AV_RB32(buf+5..8).
limitations: Palette-only disclosure (line 37 short read then memcpy of pal) is not reachable: a short avio_read sets eof_reached, and the loop exits at line 21 before any pal copy; only the same-iteration buf paths are exploitable.

The amount of stack memory disclosed depends on residual stack contents (e.g., uninit buf[5..8] must read as 0 for a zero-size frame packet to be emitted); the uninitialized USE is unconditional, but leak size is environment-dependent.

A potential infinite loop on a non-EOF read error (avio_read returning an error while url_feof stays false) is speculative: the AVIOContext fill path sets eof_reached on read errors, and no in-code producer of a persistent non-EOF error can be quoted.
No out-of-bounds write exists: 'if(size > 0xFFFFFF)' caps size, and all memcpy/avio_read destinations fit exactly within the av_new_packet allocation of size + DXA_EXTRA_SIZE + pal_size.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability instantiated in this code. The only memory write, table[i], is provably bounded by the loop guard 'i < 256 + 2*YUVRGB_TABLE_HEADROOM', which exactly matches the declared array extent, and all offset arithmetic (cb, inc) is carried in 64-bit types, preventing overflow/truncation. The remaining concern — whether computed table pointers stay inside the y_tab allocation — depends on the caller's allocation sizing and the consumer dereferences, neither of which is present in this code, so no out-of-bounds impact can be triggered here.

assumptions: YUVRGB_TABLE_HEADROOM is a non-negative constant macro (it is declared in the array dimension and reused verbatim in the loop bound, so the two cannot diverge).
av_clip(v, min, max) clamps v into [min, max] per its universally known FFmpeg semantics; this is the clamp guard bounding cb's first factor to [0, 255].
limitations: The pointers stored into table[] (y_table = y_tab - elemsize*(inc>>9), plus elemsize*((clip*inc)>>16)) are only safe if the buffer behind y_tab is allocated by the caller with matching headroom; that allocation site and the later consumers that dereference table[] are not shown, so an out-of-bounds access through these pointers would be a defect in that unseen code, not provable here.
Historical note: FFmpeg's older fill_table used 32-bit arithmetic for cb/inc, which was an overflow defect; this snippet already uses int64_t for both, i.e., the fixed form.

A negative or extremely large inc (|inc| on the order of 2^56+) could make cb overflow int64_t or push pointer arithmetic far out of object; no statement in this code produces such an inc, and the parameter is an internal contract of a static helper, so this trigger is speculative.

verdict.summary: The function carefully copies resolver-result-derived strings (lb_policy_name, service_config_json) via gpr_strdup before destroying chand->resolver_result, so the dangling-pointer hazard the code itself comments about is provably guarded; reference/unref pairs, loop bounds (i < addresses->num_addresses), and NULL checks are balanced and correctly ordered. All remaining candidates (NULL pointer.p deref, GRPC_ERROR_NONE element in the refs array of GRPC_ERROR_CREATE_REFERENCING, grpc_service_config_create on a NULL string) depend on behavior of internal callees not shown or on pointer values this code never produces, so their triggers cannot be instantiated from the given code.

assumptions: grpc_lb_policy_check_connectivity(exec_ctx, lb_policy, &state_error) fully overwrites state_error (possibly with GRPC_ERROR_NONE) when lb_policy != NULL; this callee is not shown, so the exact value of state_error on the success path is an assumption.
GRPC_ERROR_CREATE_REFERENCING and GRPC_ERROR_UNREF tolerate GRPC_ERROR_NONE elements/operands (e.g., refs[] in the disconnect path when state_error was reset); unshown internal semantics.
gpr_strdup(NULL) returns NULL; grpc_service_config_create's behavior on NULL input is unknown (callee not shown).

grpc_channel_args_find returns an arg whose ->value.pointer.p for GRPC_ARG_LB_ADDRESSES is non-NULL and of type grpc_lb_addresses; only the type is asserted in this code (GPR_ASSERT(channel_arg->type == GRPC_ARG_POINTER)).
grpc_lb_policy_create returns NULL for an unknown policy name (fail-closed assumption for the state_error/TRANSIENT_FAILURE path); callee not shown.
limitations: Potential NULL dereference: addresses = channel_arg->value.pointer.p is used without a NULL check (addresses->num_addresses in the loop); trigger requires the unshown resolver code to emit a NULL pointer arg for GRPC_ARG_LB_ADDRESSES — not producible by statements in this code, so speculative.

In the disconnect else-branch, refs[] = {error, state_error} can contain GRPC_ERROR_NONE (when error == GRPC_ERROR_NONE with chand->resolver == NULL, or when check_connectivity reset state_error); whether GRPC_ERROR_CREATE_REFERENCING mishandles NONE elements is decided in unshown callee code — speculative.
GPR_ASSERT on channel-arg type is an abort on internal contract violation (same-privilege crash, no corruption); treated as robustness, not a vulnerability.

verdict.summary: Within this snippet, the only memory sinks (utility[i] read, utility_inc[i] write) are correctly bounded by the loop guard `i < elbg->numCB` on every iteration. The narrow-int product `numCB*utility[i]` (potential signed overflow, CWE-190 in context) and the int64-to-element store at line 8 are arithmetic-quality defects whose security impact depends entirely on producers/consumers outside the given code, so no impact chain is instantiated here.

Exported JNI handler Java_sun_reflect_ConstantPool_getFieldAtIfLoaded0 receives a caller-controlled jint cpIndex (line 2) and passes it unvalidated into the constant-pool indexed accessor getFieldAt (line 4). No bounds, sign, or range check on cpIndex exists anywhere in this code, so a Java caller across the JNI trust boundary can supply a negative or oversized index that is consumed as an array index in native VM memory, causing an out-of-bounds access in the higher-privileged host process.

evidence.snippet: return getFieldAt(env, constantPoolOop, cpIndex, J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_JIT_COMPILE_TIME | J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_THROW_ON_FAIL);
evidence.reason: Sink: the raw, unvalidated attacker-supplied index cpIndex is passed into the constant-pool indexed lookup getFieldAt with no bounds/sign check on any path in this code. A Java caller invoking this exported JNI method with cpIndex = -1 or cpIndex = 2^31-1 reaches this statement with those exact values (the only intervening statements are the constant flag OR), and the index is consumed by the indexed accessor in native memory — an out-of-bounds access in the privileged VM process triggered entirely by caller-controlled input.

evidence.snippet: Java_sun_reflect_ConstantPool_getFieldAtIfLoaded0(JNIEnv *env, jobject unusedObject, jobject constantPoolOop, jint cpIndex)
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: cpIndex is declared as a full-range signed 32-bit jint parameter of an exported JNI handler, i.e. caller-controlled data crossing the Java/native trust boundary, with no documented or enforced domain restriction.

assumptions: getFieldAt is an internal OpenJ9 constant-pool accessor that consumes its third argument as an index ('get...At' semantics); its actual bounds-checking behavior is not shown and is treated per discipline 3's call-site rule: passing an attacker-derived raw index into an indexing operation with no validation in this code is a defect at this call site.
constantPoolOop is assumed to be unwrapped/validated by JNI/callee machinery not shown; no precondition about it is quoteable in this code.
limitations: constantPoolOop NULL or wrong-type would at worst crash the same process at equal privilege inside the unshown callee; impact chain not instantiated here, so recorded as robustness, not a vulnerability.

J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_THROW_ON_FAIL only selects NULL-vs-exception on resolution failure (the documented 'IfLoaded' semantic) and does not present any security/verification state; not a fail-open defect.
The concrete out-of-bounds read/write mechanics occur inside getFieldAt, which is not given; the call-site defect and trigger are fully instantiated, but the exact primitive depends on that callee.

verdict.summary: is_path_safe validates only the entry pathname string for absolute paths and '..' components, but never inspects entry type or symlink/hardlink targets, and the extraction flags (ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_TIME | ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_PERM) omit ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_SYMLINKS. An attacker-supplied tar containing a symlink entry (e.g. 'link -> /etc') followed by an entry 'link/cron.d/pwn' passes the first-pass check; archive_write_header then follows the symlink and writes attacker-controlled data to arbitrary paths outside dest_path.

evidence.reason: Sink: extraction of archive entries with no validation of entry type or symlink target and no ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_SYMLINKS option (flags set at line 80 to ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_TIME | ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_PERM). A tar with entry 1 = symlink 'link' -> '/etc' and entry 2 = regular file 'link/cron.d/pwn' passes the first-pass is_path_safe check on both pathnames, then archive_write_header follows dest_path/link and writes attacker-controlled bytes to /etc/cron.d/pwn — arbitrary file write outside the destination directory.

Origin of the incomplete guard: the only validation performed on attacker-controlled archive pathnames is a string check for an absolute prefix and exact '..' path components. It never examines the entry type, archive_entry_symlink target, or hardlink target, so a symlink entry whose own pathname is safe can redirect subsequent 'safe' pathnames anywhere on the filesystem.

assumptions: libarchive disk-writer semantics per documentation: without ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_SYMLINKS, non-symlink entries are created through any symlink already present in the extraction tree, including symlinks the archive itself just created; this is a characterizable standard-library behavior, not a project-internal assumption.
dest_path (argv[2]) is operator-supplied and not attacker-controlled content.
limitations: TOCTOU: the archive is re-opened and re-read for the second pass (lines 127-132) and the second pass performs no is_path_safe re-check, so a file swapped between passes would also bypass validation; this requires an attacker able to interleave a filesystem write between two ordered operations and was not needed for the primary finding.
strdup at line 178 can return NULL on allocation failure, making strtok(NULL, "/") undefined; environment-triggered only (CWE-690-style robustness), not attacker-instantiated.
ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_PERM restores attacker-chosen file modes (potentially setuid bits); hardening concern, not an instantiated corruption primitive.
Truncating snprintf to PATH_MAX (512) at line 142 can silently shorten very long entry names, but the destination prefix is preserved and no escape path was instantiated from truncation alone.

verdict.summary: All memory accesses in this PE entrypoint-scanning helper are provably in bounds: the 512-byte stack buffer is fully read-validated by the `r_buf_read_at(...) != sizeof(b)` error-return, and the scan loop bound `i < 512 - 16` keeps the furthest access b[i+7] at index <= 502 inside the 512-byte buffer; the follow_offset offsets (367, i+7 <= 502) are always within the buffer size passed alongside them. The single unchecked value, the return of r_bin_pe_get_entrypoint dereferenced as entry->paddr, has a NULL-trigger that can only be produced by a callee not shown, so no fully instantiated vulnerability exists in this code.

assumptions: PE_(r_bin_pe_get_entrypoint) is a project-internal callee not shown; whether it can return NULL or produce an out-of-domain paddr is unquotable from this code.

follow_offset is a project-internal callee not shown; this code passes offset values provably < the buffer size (367 and i+7 <= 502 vs sizeof(b) = 512), so any in-callee misbehavior is outside this code's instantiable surface.
r_buf_read_at is relied on per standard container semantics: bounded read returning the number of bytes actually read.
limitations: entry (result of r_bin_pe_get_entrypoint) is dereferenced at `entry->paddr` in the r_buf_read_at call and in pe_printf without a NULL check; if the not-shown callee can return NULL on a malformed PE, this yields a NULL-pointer read/crash in the file parser (speculative: precondition not instantiable from the given code). A one-line `if (!entry) return NULL;` after line 8 would remove it.
If a future/other version of follow_offset reads past its size argument or writes through the entry pointer, the defect would live in that callee; the call sites here pass in-range offsets.

verdict.summary: png_zalloc is the zlib allocation callback. The only attacker-influenced input is `items` (zlib derives it from the decoded stream, e.g. window sizing), and the quoted guard `if (items > PNG_UINT_32_MAX/size) ... return (NULL);` provably bounds `num_bytes = (png_uint_32)items * size` to <= PNG_UINT_32_MAX for every size >= 1, with the error arm returning before the allocation and memset sinks; allocation and every memset length derive from the same `num_bytes` expression, and `if (ptr == NULL) return` precedes the memsets. Two residual defects are not attacker-triggerable: PNG_UINT_32_MAX/size divides by zero only if zlib calls zalloc with size==0 (zlib's documented call sites pass sizeof constants >= 1), and `save_flags=p->flags` dereferences before the `if (png_ptr == NULL)` check, but png_ptr is the opaque pointer libpng itself registered with zlib, never attacker-supplied.

assumptions: PNG_UINT_32_MAX is 0xFFFFFFFF and png_uint_32 is a 32-bit unsigned type, making the quoted `items > PNG_UINT_32_MAX/size` guard an exact bound on the 32-bit product.
zlib (universally known library, discipline 3) invokes zalloc only with size arguments that are sizeof constants or sizeof(Bytef)==1, never 0.
limitations: Divide-by-zero (CWE-369) at `if (items > PNG_UINT_32_MAX/size)` if size==0 — trigger requires a zlib behavior (zalloc with size 0) that does not occur in any documented call path; defensive `size == 0` check is absent but the precondition is not attacker-instantiable.

Read-before-NULL-check: `png_uint_32 save_flags=p->flags;` executes before `if (png_ptr == NULL)`, so a NULL opaque pointer would crash at line 5; the later NULL check is dead for this purpose. Only triggerable if libpng registers a NULL opaque pointer with zlib, which is an internal contract, not attacker data — robustness issue only.

verdict.summary: ProcXResQueryResourceBytes declares the stack variable 'ConstructResourceBytesCtx ctx' with no initializer and contains no statement anywhere that initializes it, yet passes &ctx to ConstructResourceBytes, copies ctx.resultBytes/ctx.numSizes into the reply written to the client, and unconditionally calls DestroyConstructResourceBytesCtx(&ctx) even on the rc != Success error path. A Destroy routine releases contained resources, so uninitialized stack garbage is treated as heap pointers and freed (heap corruption in the privileged X server), and uninitialized stack data can be disclosed via WriteToClient; any connected X client can trigger it with a single request.

evidence.snippet:
int                          rc;
     ConstructResourceBytesCtx    ctx;
evidence.reason: Origin: 'ctx' is declared with no initializer and is never assigned or zeroed anywhere in this code before use (the only earlier reference, 'sizeof(ctx.specs[0])' at line 9, does not write). The whole struct therefore holds uninitialized stack memory when consumed.

evidence.snippet:
.length = bytes_to_int32(ctx.resultBytes),
            .numSizes = ctx.numSizes
evidence.reason: Sink: uninitialized members ctx.resultBytes and ctx.numSizes are copied into the reply that WriteToClient sends back to the requesting (attacker) client, disclosing uninitialized stack memory whenever the callee has not populated every member.

evidence.snippet:
DestroyConstructResourceBytesCtx(&ctx);

    return rc;
evidence.reason: Primary sink: DestroyConstructResourceBytesCtx(&ctx) runs unconditionally, including on the 'rc != Success' error path that the code itself handles via 'if (rc == Success)', where no statement in this code has initialized ctx. A Destroy routine frees/releases the resources the struct contains, so it frees uninitialized (stack-garbage) pointers, yielding an arbitrary/invalid free and heap corruption in the X server process, triggerable by any X client's request.

assumptions: ConstructResourceBytes is an internal callee whose source is not shown; per GUARD ANCHORING, the claim that it fully initializes every member of ctx on all return paths (including error paths) is an unquotable contract and was not used to dismiss the uninitialized-ctx finding; the code's own 'if (rc == Success)' branch proves non-Success returns are an expected outcome that still reaches the unconditional Destroy.

sizeof(ctx.specs[0]) is assumed to be 8 (two CARD32 fields per resource-id spec) for the overflow analysis; the quoted guard 'stuff->numSpecs > UINT32_MAX / sizeof(ctx.specs[0])' is correct for any sizeof >= 2, so this assumption does not affect the verdict.
REQUEST_FIXED_SIZE and REQUEST_AT_LEAST_SIZE are assumed to enforce the standard X-protocol request-length validation; both precede the spec-buffer use in execution order.
limitations: Lines 14-15 are a syntactically corrupted fragment (an 'if' condition whose head is missing, referencing the specs pointer and returning BadAlloc); its exact semantics cannot be recovered, but its visible body performs no initialization of ctx, so it cannot supply the missing guard.

Candidate not confirmed: line 19 passes the attacker-controlled request field 'stuff->client' as the first argument to ConstructResourceBytes. In the upstream X-Resource code this parameter is a ClientPtr, which would make this an attacker-supplied value used as a pointer (CWE-822); however, the callee's signature is not part of the given code, so the pointer-dereference impact could not be instantiated per STEP 4 and this remains speculative.

Memory-corruption/failure outcomes that depend only on internal allocation failure inside the not-shown callee (e.g., BadAlloc under memory pressure) are environment-driven and were not counted as separate findings.

verdict.summary: No trigger with an instantiated impact chain exists within this code. The oap-derived line numbers and line_count are consumed only by internal callees (u_save, format_lines, beginline) whose validation is not shown and not characterizable; the two in-code cursor uses are guarded in execution order by 'curwin->w_cursor.lnum < curbuf->b_ml.ml_line_count' before the increment and 'check_cursor();' after the saved-cursor restore. The unclamped adjustment 'wp->w_old_cursor_lnum += old_line_count;' (old_line_count can be negative) can produce out-of-range line numbers, but the values are consumed by redraw code outside this snippet, so the impact chain is not instantiated here.

assumptions: oap->start.lnum, oap->end.lnum, oap->line_count, and oap->cursor_start are produced by Vim's operator machinery (do_pending_operator) not shown; this code neither documents nor asserts preconditions on them (no quotable contract), but no trust boundary per the attacker model is crossed by their content since they originate from the same operator's command session.

u_save, format_lines, beginline, check_cursor, msgmore, and redraw_curbuf_later are project-internal callees whose behavior (including their own bounds checking on linenr/line_count arguments) is not shown and could not be characterized per discipline 3.

w_old_cursor_lnum and w_old_visual_lnum are assumed to be initialized/reset in tandem (both zero or both valid) by screen.c code not shown; this code cannot produce the asymmetric state where one is 0 and the other non-zero.
limitations: 'wp->w_old_cursor_lnum += old_line_count;' / 'wp->w_old_visual_lnum += old_line_count;': old_line_count = curbuf->b_ml.ml_line_count - <pre-format line count> can be negative (e.g., gq joining 100 lines into 10 yields -90), and no clamp or range check exists anywhere in this function (verified by searching all fix forms: range check, clamp, validity test). An adjusted value can become <= 0 or exceed ml_line_count, and w_old_visual_lnum is modified without its own '!= 0' sentinel test. If the downstream redraw code (screen.c, not shown) indexes memory with these values (e.g., plines()/ml_get()), this would be an out-of-bounds read; the impact link is outside the given code, so this is recorded rather than reported.

'format_lines(oap->line_count, keep_cursor)' and 'u_save((linenr_T)(oap->start.lnum - 1), (linenr_T)(oap->end.lnum + 1))' pass oap-derived counts/line numbers without in-function validation; a malformed oap (start.lnum == 0, negative line_count) would be harmful only if the unseen callees lack their own checks, and no statement in this code produces such an oap.

'curwin->w_cursor = oap->cursor_start;' copies a caller-supplied position that this code never initializes; the value is dead-stored (overwritten by 'curwin->w_cursor = oap->start;' before any use) and the later restore path is guarded by 'check_cursor();', but if u_save were to read w_cursor, an unvalidated position could reach it.

'++curwin->w_cursor.lnum;' assumes w_cursor.lnum is valid entering the statement; validity depends on the unshown callee format_lines, though the increment itself is correctly bounded by 'curwin->w_cursor.lnum < curbuf->b_ml.ml_line_count' (<, not <=).

verdict.summary: Off-by-one bounds check in pktRemoveEvidence: the guard `idx <= area->evidence().size()` permits idx == size(), so a remote client sending an evidence index equal to the list length (e.g. '1' with one evidence item) passes validation and is passed to area->deleteEvidence(idx), which indexes one past the last valid element, causing an out-of-bounds access (OOB read/undefined behavior) in the server process.

evidence.snippet:
if (is_int && idx <= area->evidence().size() && idx >= 0) {
        area->deleteEvidence(idx);
evidence.reason: Off-by-one: the bounds test uses `<=` instead of `<`, so idx == area->evidence().size() (attacker-controlled via argv[0] from the network packet, e.g. "1" when evidence().size() == 1) passes validation and is passed unclamped to deleteEvidence(), indexing one past the last valid element — out-of-bounds access triggered directly by remote packet content.

assumptions: deleteEvidence(int) indexes/removes the evidence list at idx; its implementation is not shown, but the call site passes an out-of-domain raw index with no validation on any path in this code, which is itself the defect.
checkEvidenceAccess is an authorization gate; a player with evidence-edit permission (the intended audience of this packet) triggers the defect.
limitations: argv[0] is accessed without checking argc > 0; whether the packet dispatcher can deliver an empty argv is not shown, so this is speculative and not counted.

verdict.summary: The attacker-controlled CARD32 field stuff->numSpecs is multiplied by sizeof(ctx.specs[0]) inside the REQUEST_FIXED_SIZE length check without any bound; on platforms with 32-bit size_t the product wraps (numSpecs = 0x20000000 gives a product of 0), so an 8-byte request passes the length validation while numSpecs remains 2^29. The specs array pointer is then derived at stuff + sz_xXResQueryResourceBytesReq (end of the 8-byte request) and consumed for numSpecs entries, causing a massive out-of-bounds read in the privileged X server process (crash/DoS and potential information disclosure into the reply).

evidence.snippet:

verdict.summary: SProcXkbSelectEvents validates the request length (REQUEST_AT_LEAST_SIZE) and, for every affected event bit, checks the remaining detail byte count with 'if (dataLeft < (size * 2)) return BadLength;' before each swaps/swapl read/write. The loop is bounded (affectWhich is 16-bit, default arm rejects undefined bits), length arithmetic cannot wrap (CARD16), and trailing data is rejected with BadLength. No guard-bypassing trigger value is producible from any input or statement in this code.

XkbMapNotifyMask corresponds to bit 1 (ndx XkbMapNotify, which the loop skips) and event constants ndx 0-11 are enumerated by the switch, with bits 12-15 reaching the default: return BadValue arm.

ProcXkbSelectEvents (callee, not shown) re-parses the request; this code hands it a request whose declared length has been validated to exactly cover the detail data under this code's own accounting, so no raw unvalidated offset/size/index is passed at the call site.

This is unreachable as written because dataLeft = length*4 - 16 is always a multiple of 4 and all consumed amounts (4 or 8) are multiples of 4; the trigger value (dataLeft in {2,3}) cannot be instantiated by any input or statement in this code. Behavior of the internal callee ProcXkbSelectEvents is not shown; if it consumed detail data with a different per-event byte accounting than this function, valid client requests could be rejected (functional issue), but this code passes it a fully length-validated request, so no memory-safety defect is instantiated at this call site.

verdict.summary: continue_send() adds the return value of qemu_chr_fe_write() to ibe->outpos without any check. On the documented error return of -1 (inducible by the chardev peer, e.g. socket backend failure), outpos becomes negative, and the next retry passes outbuf + outpos (pointer before the buffer) with length outlen - outpos > sizeof(outbuf) to qemu_chr_fe_write, producing an out-of-bounds read whose bytes are transmitted to the peer; repeated error returns decrement outpos without bound. No statement anywhere in the code clamps or checks outpos.

evidence.reason: Unchecked return of qemu_chr_fe_write (documented to return -1 on error, 0 on no progress) is accumulated into outpos. With outpos=1, outlen=2, an error return of -1 makes outpos=0 (line 9's `outpos < outlen` is still true, scheduling a retry); a second -1 makes outpos=-1, so the next send passes `outbuf - 1` as the source pointer and `outlen - outpos = outlen + 1` as the length — an out-of-bounds read (with data sent to the chardev peer) and unbounded further decrement of outpos on repeated errors. No lower bound, clamp, or return-value check exists anywhere on any path; the only reset `ibe->outpos = 0;` is inside the `outpos >= outlen` branch which negative outpos never reaches.

assumptions: ibe->outbuf is a fixed-size array (size not shown); OOB follows solely from negative outpos pointing before the buffer.

limitations: If qemu_chr_fe_write repeatedly returns 0, the code re-arms a 10ms timer and retries forever; this is a self-liveness issue in the emulated device, not attacker-scalable amplification.
No write primitive arises: outlen - outpos stays positive once outpos < 0; the impact is out-of-bounds read / disclosure, not memory write.

The subtraction 'file->buffer - file->limit' subtracts the end-of-buffer pointer (limit) from the start (buffer), producing a negative pointer difference for any buffer with >= 1 byte; assignment to size_t wraps it modulo 2^N to a huge value (buffer of n bytes yields 2^N - n). Trigger is instantiated by this code's own flow: any non-empty mem-backend hFILE passes the backend check and reaches this line, delivering a SIZE_MAX-scale length to the caller. The correct expression (file->limit - file->buffer) appears nowhere in the code.

assumptions: hFILE field semantics (buffer = start of buffer region, limit = end, hence limit >= buffer) come from the htslib hFILE structure definition, which is not shown in the snippet; the underflow direction follows from these standard semantics.
The downstream consumer of *length (e.g., a memcpy/loop in the caller of this exported API) is not shown; the direct instantiated defect in this code is the wrapped size_t value itself.

The format string has no width limit and no length check on `optarg` exists on any path, so an option argument longer than 9 bytes writes past the end of `dr` in main's stack frame — an out-of-bounds write with attacker-controlled content and length.

evidence.reason: Root cause: `%s` in sscanf performs an unbounded token copy into the 10-byte stack array `dr`. Trigger: invoking the program with `-s` followed by any token longer than 9 characters (e.g. 20 'A's) makes sscanf write 21 bytes into `dr`, corrupting the stack frame — memory corruption with attacker-controlled content. The identical defect is instantiated verbatim at lines 105-106 (`-f`), 119-120 (`-b`), and 133-134 (`-l`). No width specifier, length check, clamp, or buffer resize exists anywhere on any path; the subsequent range checks (`format < 1 || format > 2`, etc.) operate on the parsed integer only after the overflow has already occurred.

assumptions: `file_ext` (used as `file_ext[format]`) is assumed to have at least 3 entries, with `format` provably in {1,2} at that point because out-of-range values set `showHelp`, which triggers `usage(); return 1;` before the indexing statement (quoted in STEP 2).

The malloc/strcpy pairs for `audioFileName`, `adtsFileName`, and `aacFileName` are correctly sized (allocation uses `strlen(source)+1`, the same expression the strcpy needs) — no overflow there.
`dec_length` division by zero if `clock()` returns the same value as `begin` (decode in <1 tick) is a robustness issue with no security impact.

Trailing-data desynchronization of ProcXkbSelectEvents: bounded by 'if (dataLeft > 2) { ... return BadLength; }' which permits only protocol padding (dataLeft is always even).

verdict.summary: The extended clipboard parser bounds all attacker-controlled values: message length (len < 4 and len > maxCutText checks), the caps-array reads (len < 4 + 4*num check before reading num U32s into a fixed 16-entry array), and each provide-branch buffer (lengths[num] > maxCutText check with a continue that clears the flag before allocation; allocation size and read length use the identical expression). assumptions: rdr::ZlibInStream (readU32, readBytes, skip, setUnderlying) throws on overrun and setUnderlying(is, len-4) treats len-4 as a byte count; the class implementation is not shown.
rdr::InStream::readU32/skip throw when fewer bytes remain than requested; the stream class is not shown.

handler->handleClipboardCaps/handleClipboardProvide only read lengths[]/buffers[] entries selected by the set bits of flags (fill loops initialize exactly those entries, indexed in bit order); the SMsgHandler implementations are not shown.
maxCutText is a trusted positive server configuration value, not attacker-controlled.
limitations: An exception thrown mid-way through the provide branch (e.g., readBytes overrun or bad_alloc) skips the delete loop and leaks already-allocated buffers; repeated messages could grow memory use, but each message is bounded by 16*maxCutText and there is no corruption.

If the client sends trailing bytes beyond 4+4*num in a caps message, or the provide loop does not consume the full compressed payload, leftover bytes remain in the stream and can desynchronize subsequent message parsing; all later reads are bounds-checked and message types validated, so the worst observed effect is connection termination (robustness).

Uninitialized entries of lengths[16] and buffers[16] are passed to handler callbacks; a handler reading entries not selected by flags would consume uninitialized memory, but that defect would live in the not-shown handler and no such read is instantiated by this code's flow.
The error-log format string uses %d with an unsigned-cast length argument; cosmetic only.

verdict.summary: The extended-clipboard parser is the post-fix TigerVNC variant: every attacker-controlled size is bounded by quoted guards before its sink — 'if (len < 4)', 'if (len > maxCutText)' bound the message, 'if (len < (rdr::S32)(4 + 4*num))' bounds the caps reads, and 'if (lengths[num] > (size_t)maxCutText) { ... continue; }' bounds both 'new rdr::U8[lengths[num]]' and 'zis.readBytes(buffers[num], lengths[num])' with the exact variable, index, unit, and operator required. assumptions: Values of maxCutText and the clipboardAction* constants are not present in the given code; they are treated as finite positive bounds/dispatch constants, which is the only role they play in the analysis.

verdict.summary: continue_send's only memory sink (qemu_chr_fe_write on ibe->outbuf + ibe->outpos with length ibe->outlen - ibe->outpos) is safe on every reachable path: the guard 'if (ret > 0)' prevents a negative errno return from corrupting the unsigned outpos, chardev write semantics bound ret to the requested length so outpos can never exceed outlen, and every completion/reset path (outlen=0/outpos=0 and outlen=2/outpos=0) re-establishes the invariant before re-entering the send label in execution order. The historically exploited defect of this function (adding a negative return to outpos, causing unsigned wrap and a huge outlen-outpos length) is explicitly fixed by the quoted guard. The outbuf index writes use the constant indices 0 and 1 with compile-time constant values, and timer arms use fixed offsets.

assumptions: qemu_chr_fe_write is characterized per its documented semantics (a write API): it returns the number of bytes actually written in [0, requested length] or a negative errno, never more than the requested length; without this, outpos += ret could in principle exceed outlen.
The declared types of ibe->outlen and ibe->outpos are unsigned (uint32_t) per the device-state struct, which is not included in the given snippet; the unsigned-underflow analysis depends on this.

Producers of outbuf content, outlen, and outpos (message-queuing code such as addchar and the command handlers in the same translation unit) are not shown; outbuf capacity (MAX_MSG_LEN + 2) is assumed to bound outlen there, but no index/length arithmetic in the given code depends on that bound.

The trigger precondition could not be instantiated from this code's own flow, so it is not counted as a vulnerability here; it would be CWE-125 if a not-shown producer ever violated the invariant.
The 10 ms retry loop on persistent chardev write failure is an environment-dependent retry, not an attacker-instantiable amplification; likewise the 4 s waiting_rsp timer is internal pacing.

No memory-safety, injection, or bypass trigger with an instantiated impact chain exists in this code.

assumptions: php_mbregex_compile_pattern returns nullptr on failure (checked here: 'if (re == nullptr) return false;') and owns/caches the compiled 're' across the throw_not_supported path.

_php_mb_regex_init_options always initializes options, syntax, and eval for a non-empty option string; a path leaving 'syntax' unset would pass an uninitialized pointer to the pattern compiler (callee not shown).

onig_search returns matches within [str, string_lim] with beg[0] >= start offset for forward search, and returns either an error <= -2 or mismatch -1 for start > end (see limitations).

The next iteration calls onig_search with start > end and, if a match were returned, the pre-match append 'out_buf.append(pos, (str.data() + regs->beg[0]) - pos)' would receive a negative length. verdict.summary: virgl_cmd_get_capset copies the guest-supplied GET_CAPSET command (attacker-data) and passes gc.capset_version unvalidated into virgl_renderer_fill_caps, a memory-filling call that receives no buffer length, while the destination heap buffer is sized only from the max_size returned by virgl_renderer_get_cap_set for gc.capset_id. The function even retrieves the intended version bound max_ver but never compares it against gc.capset_version, so a guest can request an arbitrary capset_version whose backend caps layout exceeds the allocated max_size, causing a heap out-of-bounds write in the host process.

evidence.reason: The heap buffer is sized from sizeof(*resp) + max_size, where max_size comes only from the capset_id-keyed query, yet virgl_renderer_fill_caps is handed the guest-controlled gc.capset_version with no length argument and no bounds check on any path in this code; the sole error arm (if (!max_size)) tests a different variable. A guest sending a capset_version whose caps data exceeds max_size induces a heap out-of-bounds write in the host.

Origin of the taint and of the missing bound: VIRTIO_GPU_FILL_CMD decodes the guest-controlled command into gc (capset_id, capset_version are attacker data at this trust-boundary intake point), and virgl_renderer_get_cap_set returns max_ver — the version bound that is never referenced again in the function — along with max_size used for the allocation.

assumptions: VIRTIO_GPU_FILL_CMD populates gc from the guest-supplied virtqueue command payload (standard QEMU virtio-gpu macro semantics); gc.capset_id and gc.capset_version are therefore guest-controlled attacker-data.
