verdict.summary: fill_table consumes the 32-bit parameter inc without any range check or 64-bit widening: y_table is offset by the unbounded product elemsize*(inc>>9), and av_clip(i-YUVRGB_TABLE_HEADROOM,0,255)*inc is computed in 32-bit int (overflowing for inc > 8421504, e.g. inc = 0x40000000 truncates 255*inc to -1073741824) before the int64 widening. As a result every entry table[i] = y_table + elemsize*(cb>>16) can point megabytes outside the caller's y_tab allocation; these entries are used as yuv->rgb lookup-table bases, so the corrupted pointers turn into out-of-bounds heap accesses during conversion.

evidence.snippet:
int64_t cb = av_clip(i-YUVRGB_TABLE_HEADROOM, 0, 255)*inc;
        table[i] = y_table + elemsize * (cb >> 16);
evidence.reason: Root cause: av_clip(...) (<=255, int) is multiplied by the unvalidated int parameter inc in 32-bit arithmetic and only then widened to int64_t, so for out-of-domain inc (e.g. inc = 0x40000000 the product 255*inc truncates to -1073741824, cb>>16 = -16384) the stored pointer table[i] = y_table + elemsize*(cb>>16) lands megabytes outside the y_tab allocation. Trigger fully instantiated: inc is a data-carrying parameter with no quoted bound, clamp, mask, or 64-bit widening anywhere in the function; every table entry becomes an out-of-bounds lookup base.

evidence.snippet: y_table -= elemsize * (inc >> 9);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted offset: the unvalidated int parameter inc is consumed as a raw byte-scaled offset (elemsize * (inc >> 9)) applied directly to the caller's buffer base pointer before the loop, with no range check, clamp, or width fix anywhere in the code; combined with the truncated product at lines 8-9 it places every table entry outside the allocation.

assumptions: av_clip(x, 0, 255) returns a value in [0,255] (project-internal macro not shown; universally-known clip semantics assumed).

y_tab points to a caller-owned allocation whose extent and headroom are sized by the caller (not shown); table is a caller array of exactly 256 + 2*YUVRGB_TABLE_HEADROOM slots matching the declared parameter dimension.
table entries are consumed as pointer bases into the y_tab allocation by the yuv->rgb conversion loops (not shown); elemsize is historically 1, 2, or 4.

The historical FFmpeg fix for this exact code widened inc to int64_t in fill_table and its callers, confirming the caller can originate out-of-domain inc (colorspace-derived, attacker-influenceable via crafted media).
limitations: The actual out-of-bounds dereference of the corrupted table entries occurs in the conversion code, which is not part of the given snippet; within the given code the corruption primitive (out-of-allocation pointers written into every table slot) is fully produced, but the final read is not shown.

Whether a specific caller passes an out-of-domain inc cannot be quoted from the given code alone; the verdict treats the function as the last line of defense for its own data-carrying parameters per the analysis rules.
table[i] slot writes are in-bounds (loop bound at line 7 exactly matches the declared array dimension) — no candidate survives there.

verdict.summary: nfs3svc_decode_writeargs validates the declared data length with `dlen < XDR_QUADLEN(len)*4`, where XDR_QUADLEN(len) = ((len+3)>>2) in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic. For wire values len = 0xFFFFFFFD..0xFFFFFFFF the +3 wraps to 0..2, so the check degenerates to `dlen < 0` and always passes even when zero bytes of write data were received. The subsequent clamp sets len = count = max_blocksize, and the while loop builds an iovec over rq_pages[] entries that contain no received data; the decoder returns success (return 1) with args->count/len up to max_blocksize while dlen is 0. This lets a remote NFS client have up to svc_max_payload bytes of stale/uninitialized kernel memory written to an NFS file it can read back (information disclosure) and can crash nfsd via page_address() on out-of-message pages.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the length-validation guard wraps. With attacker-supplied len = 0xFFFFFFFD, XDR_QUADLEN(len)*4 = ((0xFFFFFFFD+3)>>2)*4 = 0, so `dlen < 0` is never true and a request with zero received data bytes passes. The clamp then sets len = args->len = max_blocksize, so the decoder accepts a WRITE declaring max_blocksize bytes of data that were never received; the loop at lines 47-52 maps rq_pages[v] pages that are not part of the request and the function returns 1 (success), leading the write path to persist stale/uninitialized kernel memory into the attacker-readable file or to crash on page_address().

evidence.snippet: len = args->len = ntohl(*p++);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: len is read directly from the network peer's XDR stream as a full-range unsigned 32-bit quantity, with no range, mask, or modulo bound applied anywhere before the wrapped check at line 37.

assumptions: XDR_QUADLEN is the standard kernel macro ((l)+3)>>2 evaluated in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic.
svc_max_payload() returns a positive value consistent with the capacity of rq_vec/rq_pages (declarations are outside the given code).
decode_fh() and xdr_decode_hyper() stay within the received head buffer (their internal checks are not shown).
limitations: The while-loop index v is bounded in this code only by max_blocksize/PAGE_SIZE; the declarations of rq_vec[] and rq_pages[] are not in the given snippet, so a direct out-of-bounds write at line 50 cannot be proven and the corruption impact rests on the (historically confirmed) downstream write path, which is not shown.

The *p++ reads at lines 14-16 could pass head->iov_base+head->iov_len on a truncated message; the sunrpc receive-side guarantee is not quotable in this code, so this OOB-read candidate is speculative.
head->iov_len - hdr at line 45 could underflow only if p advanced beyond the head end (same speculative precondition as above).
args->stable is not range-checked here; its consumer is not shown.

verdict.summary: flashsv2_prime inflates attacker-controlled compressed data into s->tmpblock with s->zstream.avail_out = s->block_size * 3 without any check that tmpblock's allocation covers that size (the same unbounded write is repeated at the second inflate). When the stream's block_size exceeds the size tmpblock was allocated for, inflate writes attacker-decompressed bytes past the end of the heap buffer (CVE-2018-7557 pattern).

evidence.reason: Root cause: attacker-derived s->block_size (parsed from the FlashSV2 frame header, unbounded in this code) directly sets avail_out = s->block_size * 3, and inflate() writes up to that many attacker-decompressed bytes at s->tmpblock. No statement in this code validates, clamps, or re-sizes tmpblock against block_size*3; the only guards are the !src NULL check and the deflateInit failure check, neither of which bounds the write. Trigger: a crafted stream whose new block_size exceeds the previously allocated tmpblock size causes a heap out-of-bounds write of attacker-controlled content.

Second write site with the identical defect: the final inflate again writes up to s->block_size * 3 attacker-derived bytes into s->tmpblock with no bound check against the buffer's allocation, so the same trigger (block_size larger than tmpblock's allocated size) produces a heap out-of-bounds write here as well.

assumptions: This is FFmpeg libavcodec/flashsv2.c; s->block_size, s->tmpblock, s->deflate_block, s->deflate_block_size and s->zstream are initialized/allocated by caller code (decode_frame / flashsv2_reinit) not shown; the allocation sizes could not be quoted and therefore were not treated as guards.

zlib semantics relied on per documented behavior: inflate/deflate write at most avail_out bytes at next_out and consume at most avail_in bytes at next_in; avail_out never increases during inflate/deflate.
src's backing buffer is assumed to hold at least size bytes as a caller-provided payload slice; this code only checks src against NULL.
limitations: Negative or oversized 'size' would wrap to a huge avail_in (uInt) and cause an out-of-bounds read of src, but producing a negative size requires caller arithmetic not shown; not instantiated.
Integer overflow of s->block_size * 3 requires block_size > INT_MAX/3, not instantiable from this code's own statements; recorded as speculative.
The unchecked return value of inflate at lines 14 and 31 is a robustness issue (error paths leave partial output in tmpblock) but does not by itself constitute memory corruption.

The triggering heap state (block_size larger than tmpblock's allocation) arises from caller-side allocation/reinit ordering not included in the snippet; the defect confirmed here is this function's absence of any bound check at the write sinks.

verdict.summary: GlyphCache::Loader passes an attacker-controlled glyph count minus one directly as a raw index to TtfUtil::LocaLookup without validating it is nonzero: when the attacker sets numGlyphs=0 in the maxp table, _num_glyphs_graphics-1 evaluates to -1/SIZE_MAX at the size_t parameter, and no check, clamp, mask, or error arm anywhere in the code bounds the index before the lookup consumes it (the == size_t(-2) sentinel test runs only after the call). The only related statement, the == size_t(-2) sentinel test, executes after the callee has already consumed the index, so it cannot bound the value; the comment on line 20 documents intent about the unshown callee but enforces nothing here. The comment 'This will fail if the number of glyphs is wildly out of range.' documents intended callee behavior but is not an enforceable guard in the given code; whether LocaLookup actually rejects SIZE_MAX (rather than wrapping in its own bounds arithmetic and reading out of bounds) cannot be verified from the code given.

Member types (e.g., _num_glyphs_graphics, _num_attrs) and the semantics of operator bool(), Face::Table validity/version parameters, and TtfUtil::GlyphCount's maxp size handling are declared outside the given snippet; _num_glyphs_graphics is assumed unsigned (any plausible typing yields -1/SIZE_MAX for 0-1).

Gloc/Glat version fields with the high bit set (>= 0x80000000) become negative ints and pass the 'version >= 0x00020000' / '>= 0x00040000' rejections, being accepted as legacy format; no version-dependent memory access occurs in this code, so no in-scope impact was instantiated.

When _glyf is false the LocaLookup validation is skipped entirely (line 21), leaving _num_glyphs_graphics unvalidated on the dumb_font path; the downstream consumers of _num_glyphs_graphics are not shown, so no impact chain could be instantiated.

The '== size_t(-2)' test checks only one failure sentinel; if LocaLookup has other failure codes, they go unhandled here, but the return value is discarded after the test, so no additional in-code impact was instantiated.

verdict.summary: In side_in_cb, the D-Bus message size 'required' is computed from the attacker-controlled 16-byte socket header via g_dbus_message_bytes_needed (which imposes no size cap; the header's u32 body_len yields sizes up to ~4GB) and passed directly to buffer_new (required, buffer) with no upper-bound validation anywhere in the function - the only guard, 'if (required < 0)', checks the lower bound. A socket peer can pin gigabytes of memory in the mediating proxy process with a ~16-byte header, repeatable per connection (attacker-scalable retention, CWE-400). Additionally, on the malformed-header path g_dbus_message_bytes_needed populates 'error' and the 'required < 0' arm never frees it - no g_error_free/g_clear_error/g_autoptr exists in the function - leaking a GError per attacker connection (CWE-401).

evidence.reason: Unbounded allocation from attacker data: 'required' is derived solely from the peer-supplied D-Bus header (documented GDBus semantics: u32 body_len with no maximum), and the only check, 'if (required < 0)', constrains just the lower bound. Trigger instantiated: an authenticated socket peer sends a valid header with body_len = 0xFFFFFFFF, so required ~= 4GB+16, the else arm allocates a ~4GB buffer via buffer_new (required, buffer), and the loop then blocks in buffer_read waiting for a body the attacker never sends - ~4GB retained per connection from ~20 attacker bytes, repeatable, exhausting the proxy process (CWE-400). No clamp, bound, mask, or cap on 'required' exists anywhere in the code.

Memory leak on an attacker-reachable path: g_dbus_message_bytes_needed (documented GDBus semantics) returns -1 and allocates '*error' for a malformed header; the 'required < 0' arm only warns and closes the side, and the function returns at 'return retval' with 'error' never freed. No g_error_free, g_clear_error, or g_autoptr declaration appears anywhere in the function. Trigger instantiated: a socket peer sends one invalid 16-byte header per connection, leaking one GError per connection with no bound (CWE-401).

assumptions: buffer_new (required, buffer) allocates a buffer of 'required' bytes and returns pointer-or-NULL (callee not shown).
side->current_read_buffer is initialized to &side->header_buffer at connection setup (not shown; the invariant is maintained by the code's own line 96).
buffer_read (side, buffer, socket) fills buffer up to buffer->size and returns FALSE on error/would-block (not shown).
side_closed (side) sets side->closed, terminating the while loop (not shown).
The authenticated message path is reachable in normal operation (client->authenticated = TRUE is set by this code at line 69 after the peer completes the handshake).
limitations: Candidate dismissed as speculative: out-of-bounds read at 'g_bytes_new (buffer->data + buffer->size, extra_data)' if auth_end > buffer->pos (unsigned underflow of extra_data). The only quoted guard, 'if (auth_end >= 0)', checks the lower bound; the upper bound is enforced only inside find_auth_end, which is not shown, so per discipline 3 it can neither produce the trigger value nor dismiss it.

Speculative: unchecked buffer_new result at line 89 can store NULL into side->current_read_buffer, which is then passed to buffer_read (line 20) on the next iteration - a NULL dereference - but deterministic triggering requires an OS allocation failure, which the attacker cannot reliably induce.
Speculative: a busy-loop (100% CPU) is possible if buffer_read returns TRUE having read 0 bytes while buffer->pos == 0; buffer_read's semantics are not shown.

Speculative: whether an attacker can keep the connection in auth mode while sending raw D-Bus messages that bypass message filtering (policy bypass) depends on the unseen behavior of find_auth_end and got_buffer_from_side; not instantiable from the given code.
GError leak magnitude per connection is small (~hundreds of bytes); impact is unbounded only across many attacker-initiated connections.

verdict.summary: jpc_pi_nextrpcl computes the precinct index pi->prcno from attacker-controlled JPEG-2000 codestream parameters (numrlvls, prcwidthexpn/prcheightexpn, hsamp/vsamp, x/y coordinates) and uses it to index pi->pirlvl->prclyrnos with no runtime bounds validation; the only bound is 'assert(pi->prcno < pi->pirlvl->numprcs)', which is compiled out in release builds and does not reject negative indices. The overflow check meant to bound the shift arithmetic reads pi->picomp->numrlvls (a stale component pointer, assigned only later in the main loop) instead of the loop's picomp->numrlvls actually used in the shifts, so it does not constrain the values feeding the index computation, allowing pi->prcno to fall outside [0, numprcs) and producing an out-of-bounds read (*prclyrno) and out-of-bounds write (++(*prclyrno)) on the heap-allocated prclyrnos array while decoding an untrusted image.

evidence.snippet:
pi->prcno = prcvind * pi->pirlvl->numhprcs + prchind;

 						 assert(pi->prcno < pi->pirlvl->numprcs);
evidence.reason: pi->prcno is computed from attacker-derived codestream parameters (prcvind, numhprcs, prchind) and the ONLY bound on it in the entire function is 'assert(pi->prcno < pi->pirlvl->numprcs);' — an assert is not an enforcing runtime guard (compiled out under NDEBUG) and it also omits any check for negative prcno. This is the missing-guard site; the minimal fix 'if (pi->prcno < 0 || pi->prcno >= pi->pirlvl->numprcs) return -1;' appears nowhere in the code in any form (no clamp, mask, range check, or error arm on any path).

Sink: the unvalidated index pi->prcno is used to address pi->pirlvl->prclyrnos (allocated with numprcs entries elsewhere). When a crafted codestream makes prcno >= numprcs (or negative via the unsigned/int arithmetic feeding lines 75-81), '*prclyrno' is an out-of-bounds heap READ and '++(*prclyrno)' is an out-of-bounds heap WRITE — memory corruption triggered solely by decoding the attacker's image.

The overflow guard checks 'pi->picomp->numrlvls' — a stale component pointer that is only assigned later, in the main loop — while the shift it is supposed to bound uses 'picomp->numrlvls' (line 37) and the main loop reuses 'pi->picomp->numrlvls' with a fresh component at line 64. A check on a different variable constrains nothing: for any component whose numrlvls differs from the stale one, the shift/product at line 36 and the r/rpx arithmetic (lines 64-65) run unbounded, which is what allows the precinct index computed at line 81 to leave the [0, numprcs) domain of the prclyrnos allocation.

assumptions: Struct field types (jpc_pi_t.x/y, jpc_picomp_t.hsamp/vsamp widths) and the pi-creation code that allocates prclyrnos and computes numhprcs/numprcs are not shown; the analysis treats all of them as attacker-influenced codestream data per the function's role as the packet iterator for untrusted codestreams.
assert() is assumed compiled out (NDEBUG) in release builds of the library; even if enabled it aborts rather than validating and omits the negative-index check.
uint_fast32_t width is platform-dependent (32-bit on common 32-bit targets, 64-bit on glibc x86-64); the wrong-variable guard defect holds on all platforms, the exact wrap behavior of shifts differs.
JPC_CEILDIV/JPC_FLOORDIVPOW2 are taken as standard ceiling-division / floor-division-by-power-of-2 macros.
limitations: Secondary candidate (DoS only): 'int xstep' (line 11) can truncate the product at line 36 to 0 or negative (e.g. hsamp=128, exponent sum 26 gives 128*2^25 = 2^32 -> xstep = 0), making 'pi->x % pi->xstep' at line 52 a division by zero (SIGFPE). This chain is fully in-code, but proving the exact marker-field ranges needed (achievable prcwidthexpn/numrlvls combos) requires the marker-parsing code that is not shown; recorded here rather than as a primary finding.

On the very first call the guard at line 30 dereferences 'pi->picomp' before it is ever assigned in this function (it is set only at line 54); whether it is stale-but-valid or NULL depends on the not-shown pi-creation code — potentially an uninitialized-pointer read, not provable here.

Unbounded iteration over attacker-declared image extents (xstart..xend with small step) is a possible resource-consumption issue, but loop bounds depend on xstep/ystep values and allocation behavior not fully visible in this snippet.

The template "%s '%s' %s %s %s" leaves slots 3-5 unquoted in the format literal, so shell safety for these fields rests entirely on the unshown implementation of stfl::quote/quote_empty (quote_empty(stfl::quote(title)) etc.). verdict.summary: dprintf_formatf never upper-bounds the field precision (or width) taken from the format string or from variadic arguments. In the FORMAT_INT path, prec is used directly as the loop bound `while(prec-- > 0) *w-- = '0';`, writing below work[0] off the stack buffer; in the FORMAT_DOUBLE path, an unbounded precision is embedded into formatbuf and passed to `sprintf(work, formatbuf, ...)` with no size check, overflowing the fixed stack buffer work[BUFFSIZE] upward. Both are attacker-triggerable out-of-bounds stack writes (as exploited historically as curl CVE-2024-6197).

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds stack write: prec is attacker-controlled (via %.*d argument or %.N literal) and is used as the write loop bound with zero-padding from w (= workend = &work[BUFFSIZE-2]) downward; no statement in the code bounds prec above sizeof(work), so prec > BUFFSIZE writes below work[0] onto the stack. Trigger: format "%.*d" with precision argument 100000 and value 42 — simulation: prec=100000 (line 119), stays after line 187, minus 2 digits at line 197 → 99998 writes of '0' starting at work[BUFFSIZE-4], running past work[0] for ~99986 bytes.

evidence.snippet: prec = (long)vto[p->precision].data.num.as_signed;
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: the precision is read directly from a caller-supplied variadic argument (FLAGS_PRECPARAM, i.e. "%.*d"/"%.*f") with no range validation; only the negative case is normalized to -1 at lines 122-125, and nothing caps the positive value that reaches the OOB write sinks.

Stack buffer overflow via unchecked sprintf: formatbuf is assembled from unbounded width/prec (lines 334-344, no check; the `left` bookkeeping at line 331 also ignores the flag bytes written at 347-353), then the formatted double is sprintf'd into the fixed-size stack buffer work[BUFFSIZE] with no bound on precision. Trigger: format "%.*f" with precision argument 200 (or literal "%.200f") and value 3.14 → sprintf writes ~202 bytes into a 128-byte stack buffer, overflowing upward over the frame; larger precisions scale the overflow arbitrarily.

assumptions: dprintf_Pass1 and dprintf_DollarString are not shown; they are assumed to populate vto/endpos with the flags and values this code branches on (FLAGS_PRECPARAM, FORMAT_INT, etc.), and any bound they might impose on precision/width/positional indices cannot be quoted and therefore does not exist for this analysis.
BUFFSIZE and MAX_PARAMETERS values are not shown; BUFFSIZE (128 in upstream curl) is assumed a fixed small constant, so any long precision (up to LONG_MAX) exceeds it.
OUTCHAR and the stream callback contract are not shown; OUTCHAR is assumed to emit to the stream and cannot write into `work`.
limitations: p = &vto[param] (line 99) with param from dprintf_DollarString or the incrementing param_num could index past MAX_PARAMETERS, but the producing parser is not shown and no statement in this code produces param >= MAX_PARAMETERS, so the trigger is speculative.

A huge width (e.g. %*d with INT_MAX) drives unbounded OUTCHAR output loops (lines 140, 217, 236, 245, 281, 287) — attacker-scalable amplification (CWE-400) whose impact depends on the not-shown stream target (fixed buffer vs. growing allocation); not counted as a primary finding.

The formatbuf[32] `left` miscount (flags written at lines 347-353 without decrementing `left`) enables a small OOB write at lines 365/368-378 when width is a 20-digit long after four flag chars; it shares the same root cause as the primary finding (missing width/precision bound).

Real-world reachability requires an application of the exported curl_mprintf family to pass attacker-influenced format strings or precision arguments; this code is judged as the last line of defense for those data-carrying values.

verdict.summary: NFSv3 WRITE argument decoder. All attacker-controlled lengths are constrained before the vector-fill loop: count must equal len, the received data length must cover the rounded-up claimed length (dlen check), and len is clamped to svc_max_payload. These quoted guards, in execution order, cap the loop's page consumption at the data actually received, preventing v from running past the populated rq_vec/rq_pages range; the XDR_QUADLEN near-UINT_MAX wrap is neutralized by the clamp, and the pre-check head overread stays within the head's backing page.

assumptions: svc_max_payload(rqstp) returns a value bounded by the transport's maximum payload (on the order of a few dozen pages), consistent with the capacity of rq_vec/rq_pages in struct svc_rqst; its body is not shown.

The receive path populates rqstp->rq_pages with exactly the pages holding head->iov_len + page_len (+ tail) bytes of the received or GSS-unwrapped record, and tail (used only on RPCSEC_GSS paths per the code comment at the dlen check) is page-resident; these paths are not shown.
decode_fh enforces an upper bound on the file-handle size (not shown), so p advances by a bounded ~88 bytes before the line-17 check.
limitations: Candidate C1 (loop index v unbounded vs rq_vec/rq_pages arrays, lines 49-54): speculative — a trigger would require svc_max_payload to exceed the array capacity or received data not resident in the page array; neither is producible from this decoder's inputs or any quoted statement.
Candidate C2 (page_address(rqstp->rq_pages[v]) on a stale/NULL page if tail bytes counted in dlen are not page-resident on GSS paths): speculative — depends on unwrapping code not shown.

Candidate C3 (XDR reads at lines 9-16 occur before the line-17 bound check): overreads at most ~88 bytes past head->iov_len but remain inside the head's backing page; the values are then re-validated and never emitted — robustness, not a security impact.

Candidate C4 (XDR_QUADLEN(len)*4 wraps for len near 0xFFFFFFFD): trigger fully neutralized by the clamp at lines 42-44, which is guaranteed to fire because line 22 forces count == len and any such len exceeds max_blocksize.

Candidate C5 (args->stable and args->offset are decoded but not range-validated here): their consuming sinks (nfsd3_proc_write, vfs write path) are not shown, so no impact link can be instantiated in this code.

verdict.summary: dprintf_formatf writes attacker-controlled precision zero-fill bytes backward from workend into the fixed stack buffer work[BUFFSIZE] with no bound anywhere in the code, allowing a stack out-of-bounds write via a format like '%.*d'/'%.500d' (and '%.500p'); additionally the FORMAT_DOUBLE branch overflows work via sprintf(work, formatbuf, ...) because the precision clamp 'if(prec > (long)maxprec)' is off-by-one and reserves no bytes for the sign or the %e exponent field.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds stack write: prec arrives unbounded from the format string (line 128 'prec = p->precision;' or line 119 va-list read); the loop writes prec '0' bytes starting at workend = &work[sizeof(work)-2] and walks below work[0]. Trigger '%.500d' with value 0: w=workend, num=0 so no digits, prec stays 500, loop writes work[B-2] down to work[B-502] — hundreds of bytes below the buffer. No clamp, bound, or cap on prec exists on the number: path (the only clamps, lines 359-360 and 376-377, are inside case FORMAT_DOUBLE).

evidence.snippet:
else if(p->flags & FLAGS_PREC)
      prec = p->precision;
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted length: the format-string precision is copied into prec with no range validation anywhere in this code; the FLAGS_PRECPARAM path (line 119) is equally unbounded, taking an arbitrary long from the va_list. This unbounded value reaches the zero-fill sink at lines 205-208 and the sprintf formatbuf at line 379/396.

Stack buffer overflow via sprintf: with format '%.*e' and precision argument 1000, the clamp at lines 376-377 ('if(prec > (long)maxprec)' — off-by-one, '>=') reduces prec to maxprec-1, but the clamp reserves no bytes for the 4-5 character exponent ('e+00') or the sign flag appended by lines 348-354/385-390; sprintf(work, "%.125e", 1.5) emits 131 chars + NUL into work[128] (for any BUFFSIZE, output = BUFFSIZE+3 chars even when the clamp fires; prec == maxprec bypasses the clamp entirely, e.g. '%.126f' of 1.5 writes 129 bytes). The assert at line 398 is CURLDEBUG-only and executes after the overflow.

assumptions: BUFFSIZE is not shown in the given code (curl uses 128); the zero-fill overflow (candidate A) is independent of BUFFSIZE since prec is entirely unbounded, and the sprintf overflow (candidate B) holds for any BUFFSIZE because the clamp never reserves exponent/sign bytes.

dprintf_Pass1, dprintf_DollarString, curl_msnprintf, and the OUTCHAR macro are not shown; Pass1 is assumed to accept ordinary format specs (e.g. '%.500d'/'%.*e') and set FLAGS_PREC/FLAGS_PRECPARAM with the given precision, which is this printf engine's documented purpose. OUTCHAR is assumed to call the stream function, not write to memory.
limitations: p = &vto[param] (line 99), vto[p->width] (lines 103, 339) and vto[p->precision] (lines 119, 345) index attacker-derived positions with no bound quotable in this code; the only candidate guard is the not-shown dprintf_Pass1 (line 35). The trigger would require Pass1 to ACCEPT an out-of-range '%N$' positional index, a callee behavior that cannot be instantiated from the given code, so this stays speculative — but if Pass1 fails to reject such indices, these are additional out-of-bounds accesses.

Unbounded width padding (e.g. lines 140-141, 217-219, 282-283) calls the stream function once per character with attacker-controlled width, allowing large output work per small format string (resource-consumption flavor), but no memory corruption.

FORMAT_INTPTR (lines 405-418) writes the character count to a caller-supplied pointer (%n semantics); this is an interface contract with the application-level caller at the same trust level, not a trust-boundary crossing by itself.

verdict.summary: In chmd_read_headers's PMGL entry loop, only the filename length is bounds-checked against end-p ('if (name_len > (unsigned int) (end - p)) goto chunk_end;'). After 'p += name_len', the subsequent READ_ENCINT calls advance p with no re-check, and for '::'-prefixed entries fixed-width comparisons mspack_memcmp(&name[2],...,31) and mspack_memcmp(&name[33],...,8/11/72) are performed with no check that name_len is at least 33 or 84 bytes, allowing out-of-bounds heap reads past the chunk buffer for crafted CHM files.

evidence.reason: name_len is bounded only for the name bytes themselves; after p += name_len the ENCINT reads for section/offset/length advance p with no comparison against end, so an entry placed near the chunk end makes the parser read past the chunk_size-sized heap allocation. Root cause: missing p-bounds re-check after each field read in the entry loop.

For a two-character name '::', name[2]..name[32] and name[33]+ are read by fixed-width memcmp calls with no guard that name_len >= 33 (or 84 for the 72-byte rtable compare). Trigger: PMGL chunk with chunk_size >= pmgl_Entries+2 containing an entry with name_len = 2 ('::') positioned near chunk end; memcmp reads up to 72 bytes beyond the attacker-sized chunk allocation, an out-of-bounds heap read (also reachable OOB via &name[33] whenever name_len < 84).

assumptions: READ_ENCINT reads an ENCINT at *p and advances p; its macro body is not shown, but the parsing loop structure (p is the read cursor) and the goto chunk_end error path imply this semantics.
pmgl_Entries is a small fixed offset (< chunk_size, since chunk_size >= pmgl_Entries+2 is enforced); pmgl fields chunk[pmgl_Signature] and chunk[pmgl_QuickRefSize] lie within the allocated chunk.

chm->chunk_size and PMGL chunk contents are attacker data: they are read from the CHM file via sys->read and the value EndGetI32(&buf[chmhs1_ChunkSize]) with only the lower bounds 'chm->chunk_size < (pmgl_Entries + 2)' and the file-size relation '(off_t)chm->chunk_size * (off_t)chm->num_chunks > chm->length' applied, both of which a crafted file satisfies.
limitations: The arithmetic 'chm->sec0.offset = chm->dir_offset + (chm->chunk_size * chm->num_chunks)' for version < 3 can overflow 32-bit before the '> chm->length' sanity check, but the result only influences a later seek offset compared against file length, and the off_t width/platform behavior needed for a concrete overflow trigger is not pinned down here; treated as speculative.
'num_entries' semantics after the goto chunk_end path ('if (num_entries >= 0) errors++') depends on READ_ENCINT internals not shown; the loop-exit bookkeeping is a robustness concern only.
Chunk_cache allocation with num_chunks up to 100000 is bounded by the explicit quoted limit, so no CWE-400 finding is raised.

verdict.summary: In keyfetch_done(), the new-key path serializes attacker-controlled DNSKEY key material (fetched DNSKEY rdata, wire-length up to ~64KB via TCP) into the fixed 4096-byte stack buffer key_buf via dns_rdata_fromstruct() with no size bound on any path and no check of the return value, causing a stack buffer overflow (or, on the truncation/error path, an empty/garbage rdata to be written into the managed-keys DB and journal).

evidence.reason: Sink: KEYDATA serialization of the attacker-supplied DNSKEY (keydata built at line 503 from dnskey parsed out of the fetched RRset) into the fixed 4096-byte stack buffer key_buf. The DNSKEY rdata length is attacker-controlled (16-bit rdlen, deliverable over TCP); no bound on the key length and no CHECK/RUNTIME_CHECK of the return value exists anywhere on the path (unlike dns_rdata_tostruct calls, which are RUNTIME_CHECKed). Trigger: malicious/replaying managed-keys zone returns a signed DNSKEY RRset containing an oversized KSK-flagged DNSKEY; verification succeeds (secure=true), matchkey fails, newkey path reaches this copy, overflowing key_buf.

Origin of the tainted value: the fetched DNSKEY RRset's rdata (content and length fully controlled by the remote zone/network peer) enters here and is parsed into dnskey, whose key material is later serialized into the 4096-byte key_buf in the newkey branch.

assumptions: Internal callees matchkey(), update_one_rr(), refresh_time(), trust_key(), fail_secure(), minimal_update() are not shown; their semantics are assumed per BIND's documented behavior and are not relied on to produce the trigger.

dns_rdata_fromstruct's overflow behavior (buffer REQUIRE assertion vs. returning ISC_R_NOSPACE) is BIND-internal and cannot be quoted; per the call-site rule the defect stands here because the attacker-derived copy length is passed with no validation on any path in this code.
The same unguarded sink also appears at lines 272-275 and 491-493, but there keydata is sourced from the local managed-keys DB (keydataset), which is bounded by prior writes through this same buffer.
limitations: zone->refreshkeycount-- (line 66) could underflow only if a second keyfetch_done for the same zone ran concurrently; the entire body executes under LOCK_ZONE and no second decrement path is quotable — speculative.

dns_rdataset_current(&kfetch->keydataset, &keydatarr) at line 330 depends on matchkey() leaving the dataset cursor at the matching record; matchkey is not shown, so a mispositioned-cursor logic defect cannot be instantiated.
now + dns_zone_mkey_month (lines 240, 358, 399, 431) wraps only at isc_stdtime_t exhaustion (~2106) — not attacker-triggerable.

If the serialization callee aborts on a REQUIRE, the immediate impact is a crash (DoS) of the privileged, network-facing named process rather than silent corruption; in builds with assertions compiled out it is an out-of-bounds stack write.

verdict.summary: The guest-controlled PORTSC_POWNER bit (line 5) routes the completion to companion_ports[port->index] with no NULL check in this code, and container_of/assert assume packet lifetime and single-completion — but none of the harmful values (NULL companion slot, freed queue, double completion) can be produced by any statement in this code; they depend on allocation, registration, and lifetime code not given, so no trigger is fully instantiated.

assumptions: port->index is bounded to the range of s->portsc[]/s->companion_ports[] by the device's port-registration code (not shown); it is set once at init and is not writable through any surface this code consumes, so it is treated as internal-trusted rather than attacker-data.
port->opaque is assumed to be the EHCIState registered at device init (not shown).

companion_ports is assumed to be allocated/populated whenever PORTSC_POWNER can be set, per the EHCI MMIO write path and realize code (not shown); this code quotes neither the allocation nor a NULL check.
The EHCI transfer core is assumed to invoke this callback only for packets embedded in a live EHCIQueue, per discipline-3-style callee semantics of the not-shown scheduler; this code cannot prove it.
limitations: Speculative: NULL dereference at 'companion->ops->complete(companion, packet)' (lines 7-9) if the guest sets PORTSC_POWNER (guest-writable register bit, attacker-data) on a device whose companion_ports array is absent or has a NULL slot — whether that state is reachable depends on allocation/realize and the MMIO write handler, neither of which is in the given code.

Speculative: use-after-free via 'q = container_of(packet, EHCIQueue, packet)' if the completion callback fires after the owning queue is freed; the free-then-complete ordering is not exhibitable in this code.

Speculative: assertion failure at 'assert(q->async == EHCI_ASYNC_INFLIGHT)' on a duplicate completion; a second complete() call for the same packet can only be produced by the transfer core, which is not shown.
